LESSONS.title: Measuring Reaction Rates: Designing a Fair Test
LESSONS.aresKeywords: rate of reaction, rate = 1/t, relative rate, fair test, independent variable, dependent variable, control variables, thiosulfate, precipitate, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: Students turn the demo times (35 s and 270 s) into rates using rate = 1/t and plan a fair test for the disappearing cross by naming the independent, dependent and control variables. This prepares them to investigate temperature in Lesson 3.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) describe rate of chemical reactions (KICD SLO a) as change in amount of reactant or product per unit time; (b) use rate = 1/t for the thiosulfate cross method and quote rate in x10^-3 s^-1; (c) identify the independent, dependent and control variables in a rate investigation.
slo.skills: Science and Engineering Practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations (identify and control variables), Analysing and Interpreting Data (convert times to rates), Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking (calculate 1/t and the ratio of rates), Asking Questions.
slo.attitudes: Core competency: Communication and collaboration as learners discuss with peers the factors that affect the rate of chemical reactions. Value: Respect, as learners listen to others' opinions when critiquing test plans. PCI: Safety and security, as learners observe safety measures when planning and carrying out activities to investigate rates of reactions.
slo.keyInquiry: How do various factors affect the rate of reactions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launched the disappearing cross demo (Beaker A at 10 C: 270 s; Beaker B at 50 C: 35 s) and defined rate of reaction, and the DQB holds the question of why B was faster. Lesson 2 gives students the tools to compare reactions fairly. They convert times to rates and name the variables so that in Lesson 3 they can test temperature. No new results are introduced here. Explaining WHY B is faster is left for Lesson 3 and collision theory.
slo.safetyNotes: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) is an irritant. Only the teacher repeats the small-scale demo, with 50 cm3 thiosulfate and 10 cm3 HCl, in a ventilated room. Everyone wears goggles. Rinse beakers straight after the cross vanishes. Keep hot-water baths away from table edges. Do not smell the beakers. Report spills to the teacher.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reopens Lesson 1: Beaker B cleared the cross at 35 s and Beaker A at 270 s. Wanjiru's DQB question, 'Why was B faster?', cannot be answered until we can compare reactions fairly and numerically. Students predict how to turn times into a single number for speed, then calculate rates from the demo times (1/35 = 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1; 1/270 = 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1). They observe the demo set-up again by examining a quantities card and sort what was the same in both beakers (50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 thiosulfate, 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, identical crosses, same observer, same beaker type) from what differed (temperature). In the Explain phase they name the independent, dependent and control variables and critique a flawed test plan. They add questions to the DQB and draft a first model note on what a fair test must keep the same. They do not yet explain why the warm beaker is faster; that is Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Students look at the Lesson 1 notebook record: Beaker A (10 C) = 270 s, Beaker B (50 C) = 35 s. Mwalimu Achieng asks, 'Time is smaller for the faster reaction. If I want one number where bigger means faster, what could I do with the time?' Individually (2 minutes) they write a prediction in their science notebook: a way to turn 35 s and 270 s into numbers where the faster reaction gets the bigger number. They also predict how many times faster B is, using their own method. Then they pair-share with a neighbour (Kiprono might suggest 'flip the time' based on his tea-brewing timing at home in Kericho).
framework.teacherMoves: Write on the board: 'Beaker B = 35 s, Beaker A = 270 s.' Say: 'Yesterday we said B was faster. Today we want a number for HOW fast.' Ask: 'If a reaction takes a SHORTER time, what should happen to its speed number?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds in silence. Cold-call 3 students (not volunteers) to share their method. Do not confirm or correct. Say: 'Keep your prediction; we will test it with the demo numbers.' Circulate and note who divides, who subtracts and who uses time directly.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction-before-instruction with pair-share: students commit to their own idea of how time relates to speed, which exposes the common misconception that a bigger time number means a bigger rate. Revisiting this prediction at the end of the Explain phase lets them see their thinking change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) writes a method in the notebook before talking; (2) can state that shorter time must give a bigger rate number; (3) notes any 'subtract the times' answers as a misconception to revisit. Tally on a class list: number using 1/t, number using subtraction, number with no method.

framework.learnerExperience: Students gather evidence in two parts. Part 1 (data): Mwalimu Achieng shows the demo quantities card on the board: 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate plus 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl in each beaker; Beaker A 10 C; Beaker B 50 C; identical black crosses on white paper; cross 'gone' when no part of the black lines can be seen from above. In groups of four they calculate the rate for each beaker with rate = 1/t: B = 1/35 = 0.0286 s^-1 = 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1; A = 1/270 = 0.0037 s^-1 = 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1. They compare with their predictions. Part 2 (observation): the teacher quickly repeats a small-scale cross test in one beaker at room temperature, and students use a stopwatch to time when the cross is 'gone', noticing that different observers disagree by a few seconds. They record the problem in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute calculators (or let students use paper). Say: 'Use only the numbers on the card. Work out 1 divided by the time in seconds for each beaker.' Walk around and ask: 'Which beaker has the bigger rate number? Does that match what you saw?' Ask: 'How many times bigger is 28.6 than 3.7?' (about 7.7, the same ratio as 270/35). WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. For the repeat demo, wear goggles, work in a ventilated room, use the small quantities and rinse the beaker at once. Ask 4 different students to say the second at which THEY judge the cross gone, and write all 4 times on the board. Ask: 'Why do our four numbers differ?' Cold-call 3 students. Do not introduce collision theory.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data transformation and noticing: converting raw times into rates shows that the same evidence can be re-expressed so that 'faster' means 'bigger number'. The disagreement between observers makes a need for agreed rules (what counts as 'gone') visible, building the idea of control before the term is introduced.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) correct calculation of 28.6 and 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1 in notebooks; (2) uses the unit s^-1 or x10^-3 s^-1; (3) can state B's rate is about 7.7 times A's; (4) suggests that a fixed observer or rule is needed when the four times differ. Check 5 notebooks while walking round.

framework.learnerExperience: Students make sense of the evidence. Mwalimu Achieng introduces the words independent variable (the factor you change), dependent variable (what you measure: the time, or the rate) and control variables (everything else kept the same). Groups return to the quantities card and make a three-column table for the anchor demo: independent = temperature (10 C vs 50 C); dependent = time for the cross to disappear (converted to rate = 1/t); controls = 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 thiosulfate, 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, same type of beaker, identical black crosses, same observer, same lighting, the rule for when the cross is gone, simultaneous pouring. Then they critique a flawed plan from 'Otieno's cousin' who used a big beaker with 80 cm3 of thiosulfate for the warm test and a small beaker with 50 cm3 for the cold test, and changed observers. They list at least three flaws and rewrite the plan. Finally they state clearly that rate here is a relative rate, since 1/t is not an absolute measure of amount per second. They also note that both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur; the rate says how fast, not how much.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Everyone stand and point to the one thing that was different between Beaker A and Beaker B.' Then ask: 'What name do scientists give to the thing we change on purpose?' Cold-call 3 students for each of the three variable names. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before calling. Prompt: 'Why must the 50 cm3 and 10 cm3 be the same in both beakers? What would happen to our conclusion if they were not?' Then hand out the flawed plan; give 6 minutes in groups. Cold-call 4 groups to report one flaw each. Press: 'Which flaw would make us wrongly blame temperature?' Reinforce: 'We say rate, never rate of heat.' Revisit the Predict phase: 'Who changed their idea about subtracting times? What changed it?' Do not explain why heat speeds up the reaction; say: 'That question is for Lesson 3 and stays on the DQB.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with error analysis: students must justify each control variable by showing how breaking it would weaken the claim that temperature caused the difference. Critiquing a flawed plan builds understanding of why fair tests matter more than simply following a recipe.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) correctly sorts temperature as independent, time or rate as dependent, and at least four controls; (2) identifies at least 3 of the flaws (different volume, different beaker, different observer); (3) explains in a sentence why a change in two things at once makes the result unclear; (4) uses the word 'rate' not 'speed of heat'. Use a thumbs-up/sideways/down check on 'I can name the three kinds of variable', and note who shows sideways or down for a small-group follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Students return to the DQB on the back wall. Each writes on sticky notes (1) one new question about how to measure or compare rates fairly, and (2) one question about what is happening inside the beaker. Examples might include 'Can we use 1/t for other reactions, like rusting of roofing sheets in Mombasa?' (inspired by Amina) or 'How would we measure the rate of uji fermenting?' (inspired by Kiprono). Wanjiru's earlier 'why' question is revisited and moved into a 'Needs the particle idea' column, and the class sorts questions into three groups: How do we measure rate? What factors change rate? Why do those factors work?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Write one question you could answer with a fair test and one you could not yet answer.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Cold-call 5 students to read and place their notes. Ask: 'Which questions can we test with the cross method? Which need a different way of measuring, like collecting gas or loss of mass?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Mark questions answered today with a green dot (for example, 'How do we get a number for speed?') and leave the 'why' questions unmarked. Say: 'These are your questions; we answer them with evidence, not by guessing.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board sorting: grouping questions by type (measure, factor, mechanism) shows students what can already be answered and gives a map of what evidence is needed next. It keeps student curiosity at the centre of the sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each student produces two notes; (2) at least half of the notes refer to the cross demo or rate; (3) students correctly place notes in categories and justify a placement; (4) at least two students link a Kenyan context (rusting, uji, githeri) to measuring rate. Record question quality: factual, testable or mechanism-based.

framework.learnerExperience: Students begin the 'My Rates Model' page in their science notebooks. They (1) draw the two beakers, label 10 C and 50 C, and write the times and rates beneath each (270 s, 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1; 35 s, 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1); (2) add a box titled 'Fair test checklist' listing the independent variable, dependent variable and controls; (3) sketch a first particle idea of what could be different inside the warm and cold beakers (a beginning guess only, using dots for particles), marking it clearly with a question mark because the explanation is still to be tested in Lesson 3. They write a two-sentence summary beginning, 'To compare how fast reactions are, I...'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model today has two parts: a measuring part, which you can finish now, and a particle part, which is only a guess.' Circulate and ask: 'What does your picture show that is different between the beakers? What is the same?' Cold-call 3 students to share their sketches with the document camera or by holding up notebooks. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before each call. Prompt: 'Both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur. How might your sketch show that?' Do not correct particle sketches; accept all and record common ideas, such as 'particles move faster' (Otieno's idea from Lesson 1), for Lesson 3 testing. Close with the exit question below.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building with revisable drafts: students record what they can already support with evidence (rates, fair test) and label what remains a hypothesis (particle behaviour). Separating the two helps them tell evidence from speculation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) both rates are correctly written with units on the diagram; (2) the fair test checklist includes temperature as independent and at least three controls with their values (50 cm3, 10 cm3); (3) the particle sketch shows some difference between warm and cold and is marked as tentative; (4) the exit slip answers 'Why is it unfair to compare a cold test in a large beaker with a warm test in a small beaker?' Collect exit slips and sort into secure / partly secure / not yet.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Before Lesson 3, check: Did students use 1/t correctly and see that a shorter time means a bigger rate? Could they explain why each control variable matters, not just list it? Which students still subtract times or confuse the dependent variable with the rate? Did the four different observer times spark a real conversation about what 'gone' means? Did any student move on to explaining why B was faster, and did I hold the mechanism for Lesson 3 as planned? Which DQB questions should shape the Lesson 3 temperature investigation (10, 25, 40 and 55 C)? Make sure goggles were worn and the room was ventilated during the repeat demo.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We calculated the rate for the demo: Beaker B (50 C, 35 s) has rate 1/35 = 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1 and Beaker A (10 C, 270 s) has rate 1/270 = 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1, so B is about 7.7 times faster. Different observers judged the cross gone at slightly different times.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Rate = 1/t for the cross method, so a shorter time gives a bigger rate. In a fair test we change only the independent variable (temperature), measure the dependent variable (time, then rate) and keep control variables the same (50 cm3 thiosulfate, 10 cm3 HCl, beaker, cross, observer).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can compare the two beakers fairly because the chemicals, amounts and way of judging the cross were the same and only temperature differed. We cannot yet explain WHY the warm beaker reacts faster; that question stays on the DQB for Lesson 3.

LESSONS.title: Factor 1: Temperature
LESSONS.aresKeywords: temperature, rate of reaction, rate = 1/t, kinetic energy, particles, collision theory, effective collisions, activation energy, fair test, thiosulfate cross

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how temperature affects the rate of the sodium thiosulfate-hydrochloric acid reaction. They use the class data table to build the first statement of collision theory, and use it to explain why warm Beaker B (35 s) was 7.7 times faster than cold Beaker A (270 s).
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) describe how temperature changes the rate of the thiosulfate-HCl reaction using the class table (10 C = 270 s; 25 C = 110 s; 40 C = 52 s; 55 C = 26 s); (b) calculate rate = 1/t in x10^-3 s^-1 (3.7, 9.1, 19.2, 38.5); (c) explain, using particles, kinetic energy, effective collisions and activation energy, why a higher temperature increases the rate; (d) state that temperature changes the speed of the reaction and not the final amount of sulfur made.
slo.skills: Predicting from a model; carrying out or analysing a fair test (independent variable = temperature, dependent variable = time, control variables = 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 thiosulfate and 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, same observer, same lighting, same beaker type); converting time to rate; plotting rate (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis); NGSS practices: Developing and Using Models, Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the importance of manipulating factors that affect the rate of chemical and biological processes in day-to-day life. Core competency: Communication and collaboration as learners discuss the factors that affect the rate of reactions. Values: Respect (respecting others' opinions in group discussion) and Responsibility. PCI: Safety and security, as learners observe safety measures when carrying out activities to investigate rates of reactions.
slo.keyInquiry: How do various factors affect the rate of reactions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launched the disappearing cross: Beaker B (50 C) lost its cross at 35 s and Beaker A (10 C) at 270 s, and the class defined rate and posted 'why' questions on the DQB. Lesson 2 taught turning time into rate (rate = 1/t) and planning a fair test with named independent, dependent and control variables. Lesson 3 uses that planning to gather evidence on the first factor, temperature. It gives the first statement of collision theory, which Lessons 4 to 6 reuse for concentration, surface area and catalysts.
slo.safetyNotes: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) is an irritant. Use only the stated small quantities, work in a ventilated room, and wear goggles throughout. Rinse each beaker straight after the cross vanishes. Hot water baths at 55 C can scald, so use a thermometer, never boiling water, and carry baths with two hands. Keep asthmatic learners at the back and let them record data instead of handling the beakers. Mop up spills at once.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reopens Wanjiru's first 'why' question on the DQB: both beakers held the same chemicals in the same amounts, so why did warm Beaker B finish so much faster? Learners predict what will happen at four temperatures, then run or analyse the fair test from Lesson 2. They use 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate and 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl at 10, 25, 40 and 55 C. Class-mean results are 270, 110, 52 and 26 s, giving rates of 3.7, 9.1, 19.2 and 38.5 x10^-3 s^-1. In the Explain phase learners use particle drawings and a Kenyan kiosk and jiko analogy (mango rotting faster in a hot kiosk, githeri cooking faster on a hot jiko) to build the first statement of collision theory. At higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy, collide more often and more energetically, and a larger fraction of collisions exceed the activation energy, so more collisions are effective. Learners place the demo's 35 s at 50 C between the 40 C (52 s) and 55 C (26 s) rows as a check on the pattern. They add new questions to the DQB and revise their first model, noting that temperature changes the speed of the reaction and not the final amount of sulfur.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their science notebooks to the Lesson 1 demo record (Beaker A 10 C, 270 s; Beaker B 50 C, 35 s). Wanjiru's DQB question is read aloud. In pairs, learners predict the time for the cross to disappear at 10, 25, 40 and 55 C and sketch a quick prediction graph of time against temperature. They also write one sentence beginning 'I think the warm one is faster because...'. Kiprono links the idea to uji and tea, and Amina to mango rotting faster in a hot kiosk in Mombasa than in a cool Nairobi home. Learners record whether they expect the same amount of sulfur at the end in all four beakers.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng points to the DQB: "Wanjiru asked why Beaker B won't wait for Beaker A. Today we collect evidence across more temperatures, not just two." She writes the four temperatures on the board and says: "In your pairs, predict the time for the cross to vanish at each temperature. You have 3 minutes. Write numbers, not just 'faster'." She gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: "Will the warmest beaker make MORE sulfur in the end, or the same amount? Think first." She cold-calls 4 pairs (one per temperature) for their predictions and records them in a class column without judging. She asks: "Where have you seen heat speed up or slow down a change at home? Mango in a kiosk? Githeri on the jiko?" and takes 3 more cold-calls. She asks learners to say what they think is happening inside the beaker, and does not reveal the answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas through a Predict-Write-Share routine. Writing a prediction with a reason before any data makes learners commit to an idea, so they can later compare it with evidence and notice where their thinking changed. Linking to mango and githeri makes everyday ideas of 'hot means fast' explicit so the data can test them.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether predictions show times falling as temperature rises (look for a decreasing time trend on sketched graphs). Note which learners predict a different final amount of sulfur and which say 'the same'. Listen for particle language such as 'moving faster' versus vague 'heat helps'. Tally on a clipboard how many pairs predict an ordering of 270 s > 110 s > 52 s > 26 s.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four with assigned roles (timer, pourer, observer-recorder, safety monitor), learners carry out the fair test planned in Lesson 2, or, where apparatus is limited, run one demonstrated temperature and analyse the rest from the class data. The controls are 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate and 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, pre-equilibrated at 10, 25, 40 and 55 C. The same observer looks down from above at the same black cross under the same bench lighting. They time how long it takes for the cross to disappear, rinse the beaker at once, and record their group time. The class pools its results into the mean table: 10 C = 270 s, 25 C = 110 s, 40 C = 52 s, 55 C = 26 s. Learners calculate rate = 1/t for each row: 3.7, 9.1, 19.2 and 38.5 x10^-3 s^-1. They notice that the 10 C row matches Beaker A from the demo, and that each 15 C rise roughly doubles the rate. They also check that the sulfur at the end looks the same amount in every beaker.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng reminds groups: "Goggles on. Small quantities. Rinse the moment your cross vanishes because sulfur dioxide is an irritant." She circulates and asks the control-variable question: "What stays the same in your beaker? Name three controls." She prompts: "Cross 'gone' means no part of the black lines is visible from above, and the same person judges every time." When groups finish she builds the table on the board and cold-calls 4 groups, one per temperature, for their times. She says: "Our class means are 270, 110, 52 and 26 seconds. Convert each to a rate using 1 divided by t. Check with your partner." After posting rates she asks: "What do you notice?" and allows WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers from 3 learners. She asks: "How does your 10 C row compare to Beaker A in Lesson 1?" and then: "Is the amount of yellow sulfur left at the bottom different between warm and cold beakers once the reaction finishes?" She notes that rates are relative rates, quoted in x10^-3 s^-1.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table construction and pattern noticing with a structured 'I notice / I wonder' routine. Building the class table from learners' own measurements, then converting to rate, shows that the pattern is real and repeatable. Linking the 10 C row to Beaker A, and then noticing that each temperature step increases the rate, moves learners from a single surprising event to a general relationship.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that groups name independent (temperature), dependent (time) and control variables correctly. Check rate calculations: 1/270 = 3.7, 1/110 = 9.1, 1/52 = 19.2 and 1/26 = 38.5 (x10^-3 s^-1). Look for learners who read the cross consistently as 'gone' and who rinse beakers promptly. Listen for statements like 'higher temperature gives shorter time and higher rate'. Note who observes that the same amount of sulfur forms.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners plot rate (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis) from the class table and describe the shape: the rate rises steadily as temperature rises. They use the graph to place the demo's 35 s at 50 C (rate 1/35 = 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1) between the 40 C row (52 s) and the 55 C row (26 s), and they check that it fits. Then, in groups, learners draw two particle diagrams of the beaker contents, one cold (10 C) and one warm (55 C). They use arrows for particle speed and show collisions, including one that is effective and one that is not. Otieno's particle idea from Lesson 1 is revisited and extended. They write a three-part explanation: warm particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often, and they collide with more energy, so a larger fraction of collisions reach the activation energy (the minimum energy needed for a collision to react) and are effective collisions. They link this to a mango rotting faster in a hot kiosk and to githeri cooking faster on a hot jiko. They also explain why both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur: temperature changes the speed, not the amount.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng says: "Plot rate on the y-axis and temperature on the x-axis. Use the class means." She asks: "The demo at 50 C took 35 seconds. Where does that point sit on your graph? Is it where you expect?" and uses WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before cold-calling 3 learners. She then says: "Now go inside the beaker. Draw the particles at 10 C and at 55 C. Show how fast they move and show collisions." She circulates and prompts: "What does more kinetic energy mean for how often particles collide? And for how hard they hit?" She introduces the term: "The minimum energy a collision needs to react is the activation energy. A collision that has enough energy is an effective collision." She avoids saying that heat only makes collisions more frequent, and says: "Warm particles collide more often AND with more energy. The energy part matters most because a larger fraction of collisions are effective." She asks Amina and Kiprono to link the idea to the rusting-roof and uji ideas they posted on the DQB, but keeps it brief and says those will be studied properly in Lesson 7. She asks: "Do the warm and cold beakers end up with the same amount of sulfur? Explain using particles." She cold-calls 4 learners and has partners rehearse their explanation aloud before writing it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling with particle diagrams and the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) structure. The claim is that higher temperature increases the rate; the evidence is the class table and graph, including how the 50 C demo value fits; the reasoning is the collision-theory model. Drawing the same beaker at two temperatures makes the invisible particle-level mechanism visible and testable against the data. Separating the speed of reaction from the amount of product avoids a common misconception.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for graphs with correct axes, labels and a rising curve. Check that learners place the 35 s demo (28.6 x10^-3 s^-1) between 19.2 and 38.5. In particle diagrams look for longer arrows at 55 C, more collisions, and at least one effective collision labelled. In written explanations check for all three ideas: more kinetic energy, more frequent collisions, and a larger fraction of effective collisions (activation energy). Flag any learner who claims warm particles are 'bigger', that the reaction makes more sulfur, or that temperature is a catalyst.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB on the back wall. They review the questions from Lesson 1, including Wanjiru's first 'why' question, and decide with sticky notes which questions the temperature evidence now answers (for example, why warm Beaker B was faster). They write new questions raised by today's work, such as: Does cooling food, for example in a fridge, really slow reactions? Does doubling the amount of thiosulfate also change the time? Why does the rate roughly double for each 15 C rise? Would crushing a solid also help? They sort questions into 'answered by temperature', 'needs another factor' and 'needs more evidence', and add today's key evidence row (for example 25 C = 110 s; 55 C = 26 s) next to the answered ones.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng says: "Wanjiru, read your first question again. Which part can we answer now, and which part can't we?" She gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then invites 3 learners to move notes into the 'answered' column with a piece of evidence. She says: "Write at least one new question on a sticky note. Start with 'What would happen if...' or 'Why does...'." She cold-calls 4 learners to read their new questions aloud and group similar ones. She points out that questions on concentration and surface area will be investigated in the next lessons, and does not answer them now. She asks Amina and Kiprono whether their rusting-roof and uji questions have moved, and says that those will be revisited in Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding. Linking questions to evidence, and sorting them by what is answered and what is not, shows learners how investigations generate new questions and gives purpose to the next factor.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that new questions are testable and linked to variables (such as concentration or size of pieces) rather than just 'why is it hot?'. Note whether learners attach evidence (a time, rate or diagram) when moving a question to 'answered'. Count how many learners have posted at least one new question, and observe whether any question already points to concentration, surface area or catalysts.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the model page in their science notebooks and revise the first model from Lesson 1. They draw the cold beaker and the warm beaker with particles, add arrows for speed, and label collisions, effective collisions and activation energy. Beneath the drawings they write a model statement: 'At a higher temperature particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and more energetically, so a larger fraction of collisions are effective and the rate is higher.' They add the evidence line: 10 C = 270 s (3.7 x10^-3 s^-1) and 55 C = 26 s (38.5 x10^-3 s^-1), with the demo at 50 C = 35 s lying between 40 C and 55 C. They also add a note that the final amount of sulfur is the same, so temperature changes the speed only. They then complete the summary table (what we observed, what we learned, how we explain it) and add one question about how their model might also explain concentration.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng says: "Your model from Lesson 1 had an idea about particles. Revise it today with kinetic energy, effective collisions and activation energy. Use a different colour pen for what you changed." She gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then asks: "What is one thing your model can now explain that it couldn't before?" and cold-calls 3 learners. She asks 2 learners to read their model statement aloud while the class checks for the three ideas. She asks: "Where in your model does it show that both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur?" She then distributes the summary table and says: "Fill in all three columns with evidence from today's table." She collects notebooks for a quick check and ends by saying: "Next lesson we change something different, the concentration of the thiosulfate, and test whether the same collision idea still works."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision using an evidence-linked model statement and summary table. Revising the same model across lessons, with colour-coded changes, makes learning visible and shows that a model is improved by evidence. Tying each model feature to a data row keeps the explanation evidence-based and prepares learners to extend it to the next factor.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that revised models include speed arrows, collisions, an effective collision and the term activation energy. Check that the model statement has three parts (more kinetic energy, more frequent collisions, larger fraction effective) and that the evidence line quotes correct numbers (270 s and 26 s; 3.7 and 38.5 x10^-3 s^-1). Look for the note that the final amount of sulfur is unchanged. Use the summary table as an exit check: learners who cannot link observed times to the particle explanation need a short follow-up with the 10 C and 55 C diagrams.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners use the class data, not just intuition, to say that rate rises with temperature? Which pairs relied on 'heat makes things faster' without evidence? (2) Did anyone say that warm particles collide more often only? If so, plan a short follow-up on energy and the fraction of effective collisions. (3) Did anyone claim that a higher temperature gives more sulfur or that heat acts as a catalyst? Note names for Lesson 4 review. (4) Were safety routines (goggles, small quantities, ventilation, prompt rinsing, safe handling of warm baths) followed? (5) How well did learners place the demo's 35 s at 50 C relative to the 40 C and 55 C rows? (6) Which DQB questions now point naturally towards concentration for Lesson 4? Note which learners need support with rate = 1/t calculations and graph plotting before Lesson 4.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe? Record the class-mean times for the cross to disappear at 10 C (270 s), 25 C (110 s), 40 C (52 s) and 55 C (26 s), and the rates 3.7, 9.1, 19.2 and 38.5 x10^-3 s^-1. Note how the demo at 50 C (35 s) fits, and that the amount of sulfur made was the same.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? Write what happens to the rate of the thiosulfate-HCl reaction as temperature rises, and how the rate changes from 10 C to 55 C. State that temperature changes the speed of the reaction and not the final amount of product.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How can we explain it? Use particles to explain why a higher temperature increases the rate: more kinetic energy, more frequent and more energetic collisions, a larger fraction of effective collisions (activation energy). Use this to explain why warm Beaker B was faster than cold Beaker A.

LESSONS.title: Factor 2: Concentration
LESSONS.aresKeywords: concentration, particles per unit volume, collision theory, effective collisions, rate = 1/t, proportional, independent variable, dependent variable, control variables, antacid tablet

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how the concentration of sodium thiosulfate changes the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid, and use collision theory to explain why more particles per unit volume give more frequent collisions. This advances the Driving Question by showing a second factor that controls speed, without changing the temperature that explained Beaker B.
slo.knowledge: Learners explain that a higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent and more effective collisions happen each second. They state that rate is roughly proportional to concentration, using the data: 0.15 mol/dm3 = 110 s (9.1 x10^-3 s^-1); 0.12 = 138 s (7.2); 0.09 = 183 s (5.5); 0.06 = 275 s (3.6). They state that concentration changes the speed, not the final amount of sulfur.
slo.skills: Planning a fair test by naming independent, dependent and control variables; measuring time to the cross disappearing; converting time to rate (rate = 1/t); plotting rate (y-axis) against concentration (x-axis); describing a trend and checking proportionality (rate / concentration is about 60); using a particle diagram as a model (SEP: Developing and Using Models; Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Analyzing and Interpreting Data).
slo.attitudes: Respect: learners listen to and value the ideas of group members when discussing patterns. Responsibility: learners take care with acid, goggles and ventilation. Curiosity about why a stronger solution reacts faster, and appreciation of how controlling concentration is useful in daily life (for example antacid tablets and cleaning products). Core competencies: Communication and collaboration; Critical thinking and problem solving. PCI: Safety and security.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Question: How do various factors affect the rate of reactions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 gave the first statement of collision theory (higher temperature means more energetic and more frequent collisions, so more are effective) and the 25 C result of 110 s. Lesson 2 gave rate = 1/t and the variables of a fair test. Lesson 4 keeps temperature at 25 C and changes a different factor, concentration, so learners see that the same collision idea (effective collisions per second) explains a second factor. It prepares Lesson 5 (surface area).
slo.safetyNotes: Wear goggles. Sulfur dioxide (SO2) is an irritant: work in a well-ventilated room, use only the small volumes stated (10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, up to 50 cm3 of thiosulfate solution), and rinse each beaker in the sink straight after the cross vanishes. Wipe spills at once; wash hands after the practical. Students with breathing problems such as asthma should observe from a distance and record data. Do not smell the mixtures. Keep all tests at 25 C and use the room-temperature water bath.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reopens the Driving Question Board (DQB) and recalls the Disappearing Cross: Beaker B (50 C) lost its cross at 35 s and Beaker A (10 C) at 270 s, with the same chemicals in the same amounts. Lesson 3 showed that temperature changes the rate. Learners now ask whether anything else besides temperature could change the time. Using the antacid tablet fizzing in a glass of water (a whole tablet in a small amount of water compared with a dilute solution) as a hook, they predict what happens to the cross time when the thiosulfate solution is made weaker, using water. In groups they run the cross test at 25 C with four concentrations (0.15, 0.12, 0.09, 0.06 mol/dm3), keeping 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, the total volume of 50 cm3, the beaker and the observer constant. Class-mean results are 110 s, 138 s, 183 s and 275 s, giving rates 9.1, 7.2, 5.5 and 3.6 x10^-3 s^-1. Learners plot rate against concentration, notice the straight-line trend through the origin, check that rate / concentration is about 60 for every row, and explain with particle diagrams: more particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions and more effective collisions per second. They also note that the final amount of sulfur depends on the amount of thiosulfate, not on the speed. The DQB is updated and the class model gets a second factor.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall Beaker A and B (35 s vs 270 s). Mwalimu Achieng shows an antacid tablet fizzing in a glass: she breaks one tablet and drops it in 100 cm3 of water. She then asks: if we kept the temperature the same but made the sodium thiosulfate solution weaker by adding water, what would happen to the time for the cross to disappear? Individually, learners write in their science notebooks: (1) a prediction (faster, slower or the same), (2) a reason with a particle sketch, and (3) a rough guess of the time for 0.06 mol/dm3 compared with 110 s for 0.15 mol/dm3. Wanjiru shares first. Learners then pair-share, and Otieno links the answer to his earlier particle idea.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson, temperature explained why Beaker B beat Beaker A. Today the temperature stays at 25 C. What else could change the time?' Show the fizzing antacid and ask: 'Think of the fizz. What would you change to make it fizz slower or faster, other than heating?' Give 1 minute silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 learners (including Wanjiru and Otieno) for predictions and record the three kinds of prediction (faster/slower/same) as tally marks on the board. Ask: 'Draw the particles in a strong solution and in a weak solution. What differs?' Do NOT confirm any answer. Say: 'We will test it, and we will keep the cross in view.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with particle sketches: writing a prediction and a reason before data exposes learners' existing models, so later evidence confirms or challenges something they personally committed to. Tally marks make the class's range of ideas visible without judging.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: every learner has a written prediction, a reason and a particle sketch. Indicators: sketches show different numbers of particles in the same volume (strong sign of concentration idea); predictions that mention 'more particles' or 'more collisions'; misconceptions such as 'weaker solution means less sulfur made faster' or 'concentration changes temperature'. Record tally counts of faster/slower/same. Note learners who link back to Lesson 3 collision ideas.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 (roles: reader, timer, pourer, recorder), learners plan and run the cross test at 25 C. First they fill a planning table in their notebooks: Independent variable = concentration of sodium thiosulfate (0.15, 0.12, 0.09, 0.06 mol/dm3); dependent variable = time for the cross to disappear (converted to rate = 1/t); control variables = 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, 50 cm3 total volume of solution, temperature 25 C, same beaker type, same black cross, same observer, same bench lighting. They prepare the thiosulfate by mixing volumes: 50 cm3 thiosulfate + 0 water; 40 + 10; 30 + 20; 20 + 30. They put the cross under the beaker, add 10 cm3 HCl, start the stopwatch, look down from above and stop when no part of the black lines can be seen, then rinse the beaker straight away. Groups pool their times with the class. Class-mean values: 0.15 mol/dm3 = 110 s; 0.12 = 138 s; 0.09 = 183 s; 0.06 = 275 s. They calculate rate = 1/t in x10^-3 s^-1: 9.1, 7.2, 5.5 and 3.6. The 0.15 result matches the 25 C row from Lesson 3 (110 s). Learners record the table.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out goggles and check every pair before any acid is poured: 'Goggles on, hair tied back, windows open.' Remind: 'SO2 is an irritant. Small amounts only, and rinse the beaker the moment the cross is gone.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which variable are you changing? Which are you keeping the same? How do you know the cross is gone?' (Cross is gone when the observer looking down can no longer see any part of the black lines.) Check that the same person judges the cross in every run. After runs, collect times on the board and compute the class mean. Ask: 'Which concentration took the longest? Does the 0.15 row match something we measured in Lesson 3?' Wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 groups to report their time for one concentration. Ask learners to convert to rates and write them in the table with units x10^-3 s^-1. Say: 'Rate here is a relative rate: 1 divided by the time.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with a shared class table: pooling results reduces the effect of individual error, shows reliability (the 0.15 row matches Lesson 3), and gives every learner the same evidence for sensemaking. Naming variables before the practical makes the fair test explicit (SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe: correct dilution volumes in each beaker; goggles worn; same observer and same lighting; timer stopped at the same cross-visibility criterion; beaker rinsed immediately. Check notebooks for correct identification of independent, dependent and control variables, and for correct 1/t calculations (9.1, 7.2, 5.5, 3.6 x10^-3 s^-1). Ask a quick thumbs check: 'Did the weaker solution take longer?' Note groups whose times are far from the class mean and ask them to suggest why (measurement error, uneven mixing, different observer).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners plot the class data on graph paper: concentration (mol/dm3) on the x-axis and rate (x10^-3 s^-1) on the y-axis, as in Lesson 2. They draw a best-fit line and describe the trend: as concentration decreases from 0.15 to 0.06, rate falls from 9.1 to 3.6, and the points lie close to a straight line through the origin. They calculate rate / concentration for each row (about 60 each time) and conclude that rate is roughly proportional to concentration: halve the concentration and the rate roughly halves. Then they explain with particle diagrams: the same volume (50 cm3) contains more thiosulfate particles at 0.15 than at 0.06, so thiosulfate and H+ particles meet more often, giving more collisions per second and so more effective collisions per second. Because the temperature is the same, the energy of each particle is the same, so the fraction of collisions that are effective does not change. Learners also compare the two ideas: temperature changed both the energy and the number of collisions (Lesson 3), but concentration changes only how many collisions occur per second. They link back to the antacid: a stronger acid solution fizzes faster. They finally decide whether the amount of sulfur at the end would differ (the final amount depends on the amount of thiosulfate: a weaker solution contains less thiosulfate but the speed is not the same as the amount).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Plot concentration on the x-axis and rate on the y-axis, as we did in Lesson 2. What does the pattern tell you?' Ask: 'Describe the line in one sentence using numbers from the table.' Wait 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'What happens to rate / concentration in each row? Calculate 9.1 / 0.15 and 3.6 / 0.06.' Guide to about 60 and say: 'This means rate is roughly proportional to concentration.' Then ask: 'Look at your particle diagrams from the Predict Phase. What does 0.15 have more of in 50 cm3?' (More particles per unit volume.) Press for the chain of reasoning: 'More particles per unit volume, so what happens to collisions? Then what happens to effective collisions per second?' Cold-call 3 more learners to complete the sentence frame: 'Because there are more ___ in the same volume, ___ happen more often, so ___.' Ask: 'Did the particles gain energy as we diluted or concentrated the solution? How do you know?' (Temperature was constant at 25 C.) Ask: 'In Lesson 3 energy changed. What is different here?' Correct any claim that a higher concentration means particles move faster. Ask Kiprono to say how a stronger cup of tea or uji mix tastes sooner, then link carefully: 'Is that the same idea? What changed, the number of particles in the volume or their energy?' Close with: 'Would both beakers still end with sulfur?' (Yes: concentration changes the speed, not the type of product.)
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with particle models: learners state the claim (rate roughly proportional to concentration), cite the data (rate / concentration is about 60), and give the collision reasoning (more particles per unit volume, more frequent collisions, more effective collisions per second). Comparing with Lesson 3 separates frequency of collisions (concentration) from energy of collisions (temperature), which prevents the misconception that frequency means energy (SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check graphs: axes labelled with units, correct plotting, best-fit line through or close to the origin. Check statements: 'rate is roughly proportional to concentration' backed with the ratio of about 60 for every row. Check explanations for the three-step chain (more particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions, so more effective collisions per second) and no confusion with energy. Ask a mini-whiteboard question: 'If the concentration doubled from 0.06 to 0.12 mol/dm3, what happens to the rate? (3.6 to 7.2 x10^-3 s^-1, roughly double).' Indicators of mastery: 80% of learners write the correct chain; misconceptions noted for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB on the back wall. They add sticky notes with new questions arising from today's work, for example: 'Does doubling concentration always double the rate?', 'Why was the 0.06 mol/dm3 time (275 s) almost the same as Beaker A at 10 C (270 s)?', 'Can a gas be made more concentrated by pressing it?', 'Why does a crushed antacid tablet fizz faster than a whole one?' Groups sort questions into 'answered today' (for example, why was the weaker solution slower), 'still to investigate' (surface area, catalysts, light) and 'new'. Learners move a question or two that were answered today into the 'Answered' column with a one-line evidence note citing the table. They keep their own copy in their notebook.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Write one question that today's data raised for you, on a sticky note.' Allow 2 minutes of silent writing and then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 learners to read a question and place it on the DQB. Ask: 'Which of our earlier questions about Beaker A and B can we now partly answer? What is the evidence?' Invite Wanjiru to revisit her first 'why' question and say what part is explained so far. Ask Amina and Kiprono whether their rusting roof and tea/uji examples relate to concentration: 'Would a more concentrated solution change how fast things happen? Hold that thought for Lesson 7.' Point out the 'crushed tablet' question: 'That one leads us straight to Lesson 5.' Accept all questions respectfully and do not answer them now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: moving questions between 'still to investigate' and 'answered' with evidence makes progress visible, and new questions create a purpose for the next lesson. Learners see science as a cycle of questions and evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count and review sticky notes: at least one question per learner. Indicators: questions that use particle language (particles, collisions, volume), questions that propose a new factor (surface area, pressure), and questions that connect to Kenyan contexts. Check that learners cite table evidence when they move a question to 'Answered'. Note learners writing only factual or off-topic questions for support.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their class collision model started in earlier lessons. On a poster or in their notebooks they draw two labelled boxes of equal volume at 25 C: a high-concentration box (0.15 mol/dm3) with many thiosulfate and H+ particles and a low-concentration box (0.06 mol/dm3) with few. They add arrows showing collisions and shade the effective ones. They add a line to the model: 'Higher concentration = more particles per unit volume = more frequent collisions = more effective collisions per second = higher rate (roughly proportional).' Under the temperature factor from Lesson 3 they add: 'Concentration changes how often particles meet; it does not change their energy.' They then use the model to answer: (a) Explain why the 0.06 mol/dm3 solution at 25 C took 275 s while 0.15 took 110 s. (b) Predict the rate if the concentration were 0.075 mol/dm3 (about half of 0.15, so roughly half the rate, about 4.5 x10^-3 s^-1). (c) Link to the antacid tablet fizzing in a small volume of water versus a large volume. They complete the ARES Summary Table and write one sentence linking the model to the anchor demo (Beaker A and B), explaining that concentration was the same in both beakers, so temperature was the cause.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add today's factor to our model. Show it with particles in equal volumes.' Circulate and ask: 'Where are the effective collisions? Where did energy change, and where did only the number of particles change?' Ask: 'Predict the rate for 0.075 mol/dm3. What evidence supports your prediction?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Then ask: 'In the anchor demo both beakers had the same concentration. Which factor explains the difference? Which factor is ruled out?' Have learners complete the Summary Table. Ask one pair to explain the model to another pair. Close: 'Next lesson: why does a crushed antacid tablet fizz faster than a whole one?' Collect notebooks or photograph models for the teacher reflection.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with prediction: adding concentration to the collision model, and then using it to predict an unseen value (0.075 mol/dm3) tests whether the model is useful, not just descriptive. Explicitly returning to the anchor demo reinforces that the model must explain the phenomenon (SEP: Developing and Using Models).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: equal-volume boxes with different numbers of particles, collision arrows, effective collisions marked, and a clear note that energy was unchanged. Check predictions: about half the rate at about half the concentration (around 4.5 x10^-3 s^-1) with the reasoning from the table. Exit question: 'Does a weaker solution make less sulfur at the end, or just make it more slowly?' Look for the idea that concentration changes the speed (more precisely, the amount depends on how much thiosulfate is present). Indicators of mastery: model uses the term 'effective collisions per second' correctly and does not use 'frequency' to mean 'energy'.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners separate the effect of concentration (number of collisions per second) from temperature (energy and number of collisions)? Which learners still say that 'stronger' means 'particles move faster'? (2) Did every group control the variables (10 cm3 HCl, 50 cm3 total, 25 C, same observer and lighting)? Which results were far from the class mean, and why? (3) Could learners explain why rate / concentration is about 60 for every row and use it to say 'roughly proportional'? (4) Did learners use the three-step chain (more particles per unit volume, more frequent collisions, more effective collisions per second)? (5) Were safety routines followed: goggles, ventilation, small volumes, immediate rinsing? (6) Which DQB questions show readiness for surface area in Lesson 5? What would you change in time management, grouping or the antacid hook next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that at 25 C the cross disappeared in 110 s, 138 s, 183 s and 275 s as the sodium thiosulfate concentration decreased from 0.15 to 0.12, 0.09 and 0.06 mol/dm3. The matching rates (1/t) were 9.1, 7.2, 5.5 and 3.6 x10^-3 s^-1. The weaker the solution, the longer the cross stayed visible.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, and that rate is roughly proportional to concentration (rate / concentration is about 60 for every row). Concentration changes how fast the reaction goes, not the type of products, and it is a second factor besides temperature.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explained that in a more concentrated solution there are more particles in the same volume, so they collide more often, giving more effective collisions per second and a faster rate. The energy of the particles did not change because the temperature stayed at 25 C. In the anchor demo the concentration was the same in Beakers A and B, so temperature, not concentration, caused the 35 s versus 270 s difference.

LESSONS.title: Factor 3: Surface Area – Why Does Powder React Faster Than Chunks?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: surface area, collision theory, effective collisions, marble chips, calcium carbonate, gas volume, gradient, initial rate, unga, antacid tablet

slo.purpose: Learners use gas-volume data to show that breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases the rate of reaction, explain this using collision theory, and read a rate from the gradient of a volume-time curve. This extends the anchor question: if temperature and concentration change how often and how energetically particles collide, what else can change the number of effective collisions per second?
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) describe rate of chemical reactions as the change in amount of reactant or product per unit time, measured here as volume of CO2 (cm3) per second; (b) explain that smaller pieces expose more surface, so more particles of the solid are available for collisions with acid particles and there are more effective collisions per second; (c) state that the gradient of a volume-time curve is the rate; (d) state that surface area changes the speed of the reaction, not the final amount of gas made (maximum about 120 cm3).
slo.skills: Perform experiments involving the rate of chemical reactions (set up gas collection, take readings every 30 s); identify and control variables (mass 0.5 g, 25 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, 25 C); record and tabulate data; plot volume-time graphs; calculate initial rate = volume/time; draw and evaluate conclusions from evidence (NGSS practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Constructing Explanations, Developing and Using Models).
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the importance of manipulating factors affecting the rate of chemical processes in day-to-day life (for example unga versus whole maize for uji, crushed antacid tablets). Core competencies: Communication and collaboration (discussing factors with peers) and Critical thinking and problem solving. Values: Responsibility and Respect for others' opinions. PCI: Safety and security when carrying out activities to investigate rates of reactions.
slo.keyInquiry: How do various factors affect the rate of reactions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3 and 4 gave us collision theory: higher temperature and higher concentration produce more effective collisions per second. Lesson 1 introduced gas volume as one of three ways to measure rate. Here learners test a third factor with a new measuring method, apply the same collision idea to a solid, and learn to read rate as a gradient. This prepares Lesson 6, where learners meet a rate change that does not come from a change in temperature, concentration or particle size.
slo.safetyNotes: Wear goggles throughout. 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl is an irritant: handle with care, wipe spills at once and rinse splashes on skin with plenty of water. Do not put powdered chalk or marble dust near eyes or breathe it in. Use a bung or delivery tube fitted loosely so pressure cannot build up. Keep the room ventilated. Report any spills or injury to Mwalimu Achieng and use the first aid kit. Wash hands after the practical and dispose of used mixtures as instructed.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reopens the Driving Question Board (DQB) and reminds the class that the cross vanished at 35 s in warm Beaker B and at 270 s in cold Beaker A, with the same chemicals in the same amounts. Temperature (Lesson 3) and concentration (Lesson 4) both changed the number of effective collisions per second. Learners now ask: can the SIZE of a solid change the rate even when temperature, concentration and amounts are the same? Using the Kenyan example of unga versus whole maize for uji and a fizzing antacid tablet, learners predict, then test 0.5 g of marble chips (CaCO3) as large chips (about 10 mm), small chips (about 3 mm) and powder in 25 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl at 25 C, collecting CO2 over 120 s. Class-mean data show that powder is fastest and levels off at 120 cm3. Learners calculate initial rates, read gradients on volume-time curves, explain with collision theory, post new DQB questions and revise their cumulative model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the anchor demo (Beaker B 35 s, Beaker A 270 s) and the Lessons 3 and 4 explanation of effective collisions. Mwalimu Achieng holds up a whole antacid tablet and a crushed one, and shows a handful of whole maize kernels next to unga. Learners individually write in their science notebooks: (1) Which will react faster with acid, a big marble chip or the same mass of marble powder? (2) Draw the CO2 volume-time line you expect for large chips, small chips and powder on one sketch graph. (3) Do you think they will make the same TOTAL amount of gas? Why? Then they share with a partner and agree on one prediction. Kiprono from Kericho wonders whether unga makes uji ferment faster than whole maize, and Amina asks if this has anything to do with the cross in the beakers.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Last lesson we saw that more particles in the same volume means more collisions. Today the acid and the chemicals stay the same. I am only changing one thing: how the marble is cut up. Before I show you anything, commit to a prediction." Hold up the crushed and whole tablet. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent writing. Then say: "Turn to your partner and compare sketch graphs. You have two minutes." Cold-call 4 pairs: "Which sample did you put highest, and what made you choose it?" Record predictions on the board in three columns (large, small, powder) without saying who is right. Ask: "What do you think is the same in all three tests?" and let learners list the control variables. Do not explain surface area yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Commit-Compare: committing to a written prediction and a sketch graph before the evidence makes learners' preconceptions visible, so the later data can confirm or challenge them. Asking about the total amount of gas surfaces the misconception that a faster reaction makes more product (linked to the anchor outcome that both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for: (a) a sketch graph with a prediction for all three samples; (b) a reason that mentions pieces, size or 'more of it touching the acid'; (c) a statement about whether the total gas is the same. Note learners who predict a bigger final volume for powder. Listen for the language of Lessons 3-4 (collisions, particles). Tally on a clipboard how many predict powder fastest.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 with assigned roles (reader, timer, gas-syringe or measuring-cylinder operator, recorder), learners wear goggles and carry out the practical at room temperature (about 25 C). For each test they add 0.5 g of marble chips (CaCO3) to 25 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl in a conical flask, quickly fit the bung and delivery tube, and record the volume of CO2 collected (cm3) at 30 s, 60 s, 90 s and 120 s. The equation is CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g). Groups test large chips (about 10 mm), small chips (about 3 mm) and powder. They watch the bubbling closely and note which sample fizzes most at the start. Class-mean results are entered on the board table: Large chips: 12, 22, 31, 39 cm3. Small chips: 28, 50, 68, 82 cm3. Powder: 62, 100, 117, 120 cm3. Powder levels off at about 120 cm3, the maximum possible from 0.5 g (0.005 mol) because HCl is in excess (0.025 mol). Learners note in their science notebooks that the mass of marble, the volume and concentration of acid and the temperature stayed the same.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting say: "Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and three control variables. Thumbs up when you have all five." Cold-call 3 groups. Circulate and check goggles, bungs and that the timer starts the moment the marble touches the acid. Ask each group: "What is your timer's job at 30 seconds?" and "How do you know the acid is the same in each test?" Remind: "Add the powder quickly and keep it away from your face." Give a 30-second scribe count so that all groups read together. Pause after the data are on the board and say: "Look at the table in silence for 15 seconds. Write one thing you notice and one thing that surprises you." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Ask: "Which row levelled off? What number did it stop at?" Do NOT explain yet. Rinse flasks and clear the bench; collect used materials in the waste container.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Data Collection with Noticing and Wondering: roles keep all learners active, and a silent noticing routine focuses attention on patterns in the table (ordering of rows, the plateau at 120 cm3) before any explanation is offered. Control-variable naming rehearses the fair-test thinking from Lesson 2.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: wear goggles and fit bungs safely; keep mass (0.5 g), acid (25 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3) and temperature the same; read volumes at the right times; and record in a neat table. In the noticing round listen for 'powder fizzed most at the start', 'powder stopped at 120' and 'large chips are slowest'. Note groups whose results differ and ask why (timing error, spillage, sample variation).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners first plot volume of CO2 (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for all three samples on one set of axes using the class-mean data, joining points with smooth curves. They compare the sketch they predicted with the real graph. Next they calculate the initial rate over the first 30 s: large 12/30 = 0.40 cm3/s; small 28/30 = 0.93 cm3/s; powder 62/30 = 2.07 cm3/s. They draw a tangent or straight line along the first part of each curve and see that the steeper the line, the greater the rate: the gradient (slope) of a volume-time curve is the rate. They explain why powder levels off at 120 cm3 while the others are still rising at 120 s (the marble in powder is used up first; all three would give about 120 cm3 eventually). Using particle diagrams, learners draw a large chip and the same mass of powder, shading the particles on the outside that can meet acid particles, and write a collision-theory explanation: smaller pieces expose more surface, so more CaCO3 particles are touched by HCl particles each second, giving more effective collisions per second. They compare it with Lessons 3 and 4 and note that here temperature and concentration did not change, so the particles' energy and the acid concentration are the same; only the number of particles available to collide changed. They link back to the cross: a larger exposed surface would let the thiosulfate cross vanish sooner only if a solid were involved, but there the factor was energy. They also apply it to uji: unga has far more surface than whole maize, so it cooks and ferments faster, and Kiprono's question gets a first answer.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Plot volume on the y-axis and time on the x-axis. Use a different symbol for each sample." Circulate and ask: "Which curve is steepest at the start? What does steep mean for rate?" Then say: "The gradient is the rate. Show me with your hand how the steep part and the flat part of the powder curve differ." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 learners to calculate each initial rate at the board: 0.40, 0.93, 2.07 cm3/s. Ask: "Why does the powder curve flatten at 120 cm3?" and cold-call 2 learners; guide: "What is limiting the gas, the acid or the marble?" (HCl is in excess, 0.025 mol versus 0.005 mol of CaCO3). Then ask: "Use the words particles, surface, collisions and effective in one sentence." Cold-call 4 learners and have the class refine one model sentence. Challenge: "Is the powder particle itself any hotter or more energetic? Where did the extra collisions come from?" Reinforce that surface area changes the number of collisions per second, not the energy per collision. Correct the misconception that more surface makes more total gas.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Model-Based Explanation: learners make a claim (smaller pieces react faster), cite evidence (initial rates 0.40, 0.93, 2.07 cm3/s; steeper curves; powder reaches 120 cm3 first), and reason with collision theory (more exposed particles, more effective collisions per second). Reading the gradient as the rate links the graph to the rate definition and connects the gas method from Lesson 1 to the cross method (rate = 1/t).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check graphs for correct axes (volume on y, time on x), labelled curves and a plateau at 120 cm3. Check calculations: 12/30 = 0.40, 28/30 = 0.93, 62/30 = 2.07 cm3/s with units. Listen for 'steeper gradient = faster rate' and for explanations that use effective collisions per second without claiming the particles have more energy. Ask three learners to explain the plateau; look for the idea that the marble is used up and the acid is in excess. Check particle diagrams show more exposed surface for the powder.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB on the back wall, kept by Mwalimu Achieng. Wanjiru reads the original question again (why was Beaker B faster?). Groups look for questions already answered and move them to an 'Answered' area with a note of the evidence (for example 'Particle size changes rate: powder 2.07 cm3/s vs large chips 0.40 cm3/s'). Each group writes at least one new question on a sticky note. Possible questions: Why do antacid tablets work faster when crushed or chewed? Does surface area matter for maize flour dust catching fire in a mill? Why does unga cook faster than whole maize? Is there a factor that speeds up a reaction without changing temperature, concentration or size? Do the factors work together? Learners place their notes beside the matching factor heading (temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst, light).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at our DQB. Which questions can we now answer with evidence from today? Come up and move one, and tell us the data you used." Cold-call 3 learners to move a question. Then say: "Write one new question that today's evidence made you wonder about, in the form 'What would happen if...' or 'Why does...'. Take 2 minutes." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 groups to read their questions aloud. Group questions by theme and ask: "What do these questions have in common?" Point out the question about a speed-up with no change to temperature, concentration or size and say: "Hold on to that one for next lesson." Thank learners for respectful listening to others' opinions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record: moving answered questions with cited evidence builds the habit of evidence-based answers, while new questions keep the inquiry going and point to the next investigation (Lesson 6: catalysts and light).
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for each group moving at least one question with a correct evidence statement from today's table or graph. Check new questions are testable and connected to the phenomenon, not simple recall. Note learners who ask about a factor not yet covered, as a sign of readiness for Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the cumulative model page in their science notebooks, started in Lesson 1 and revised in Lessons 3 and 4. They add a third panel: 'Surface area'. Using particle drawings, they show a large chip with few exposed particles and powder with many exposed particles, with acid particles colliding at the surface. They label 'more surface = more effective collisions per second'. In a summary line they write that temperature changes the energy and frequency of collisions, concentration changes how crowded the particles are, and surface area changes how many solid particles can be reached. They add the evidence from the table: initial rates 0.40, 0.93 and 2.07 cm3/s, and the gradient idea. They revisit the anchor demo and write one sentence on why the warm Beaker B (35 s) beat cold Beaker A (270 s), 7.7 times faster, with the same chemicals and same final amount of sulfur. They also note one limit of the model: surface area did not change the final volume (120 cm3). Finally they write a short real-life application: why unga cooks faster than whole maize or why a crushed antacid tablet acts quickly, and one safety idea such as keeping flour dust away from flames. Learners share their models with a partner and give one piece of kind feedback.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Open your model page. Add a new panel for surface area. Draw the chip, the powder and the acid particles, and label where collisions happen." Circulate with the question: "Where on this drawing can an acid particle actually hit a marble particle?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before pairs share. Cold-call 3 learners to explain their panel using the words particles, surface and effective collisions. Then say: "Now connect all three factors so far. In one sentence, what do they all change?" Guide to 'the number of effective collisions per second'. Ask: "What does surface area NOT change?" (total amount of product). Collect 3 exit tickets: 'Powder fastest because...' and 'The gradient of a volume-time curve is...'. Preview Lesson 6: "Next lesson we will see a reaction speed up with no change to temperature, concentration or size."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: learners extend the same particle model across factors, which shows the unifying idea of effective collisions per second, and they test the model against the anchor demo. Stating the limits of the model (final amount unchanged) strengthens scientific reasoning and prepares for the catalyst lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the model panel for: more exposed particles on powder, labelled collisions at the surface, the phrase effective collisions per second, and evidence figures (0.40, 0.93, 2.07 cm3/s). Check the exit ticket: powder is fastest because it has the largest surface area, and the gradient equals the rate. Note learners who still say a bigger surface gives more product; follow up with the 120 cm3 plateau. Check the anchor-demo sentence matches the facts (35 s vs 270 s, 7.7 times).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners explained the rate difference with surface and collisions rather than saying 'powder is smaller so it is quicker'? Did groups control the variables (0.5 g, 25 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, 25 C) and time the first 30 s carefully, since initial rate depends on it? Did anyone confuse the steeper gradient with a larger final volume, or claim the powder particles have more energy? Which graphs had wrong axes or no plateau? Did the DQB questions hint at readiness for catalysts? What would I change: more practice reading gradients, a shorter practical so more time for discussion, or an extra Kenyan example such as flour dust or crushed antacid? Record learners who need support with plotting and calculations.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Powder fizzed fastest and levelled off at 120 cm3 of CO2; small chips were next; large chips were slowest. Initial rates over the first 30 s were 0.40 cm3/s (large), 0.93 cm3/s (small) and 2.07 cm3/s (powder).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area, so more particles can collide with acid particles and the rate rises. The gradient of a volume-time curve gives the rate. Surface area changes the speed, not the final amount of gas (maximum about 120 cm3).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: With the same mass, acid and temperature, powder exposes more CaCO3 particles to HCl particles, so there are more effective collisions per second and a steeper curve. This is the same collision idea used for temperature and concentration, and it helps explain why unga cooks faster than whole maize and why a crushed antacid works quickly.
