LESSONS.title: Factor 4: Catalysts and Light
LESSONS.aresKeywords: catalyst, enzyme, catalase, activation energy, alternative pathway, effective collisions, light energy, photosynthesis, Haber process, hydrogen peroxide

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how a catalyst changes the rate of a reaction without a change in temperature, concentration or size of pieces, and use collision theory to explain why. They also recognise that light supplies energy for some reactions. This answers the phenomenon question of what controls speed inside the beaker and extends it to the enzymes in the human gut and to industry.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) describe rate of chemical reactions; (c) explain factors that influence the rate of reactions in biological, chemical and physical processes (catalyst and light). Specifically: a catalyst, such as the enzyme catalase in liver, speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy (the minimum energy needed for a collision to react) and is not used up. An enzyme is a biological catalyst. Light is a source of energy for some reactions (photosynthesis, silver bromide in photographic film) and is not a catalyst. Factors change the speed of a reaction, not the final amount made.
slo.skills: NGSS SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations (identify independent, dependent and control variables in the catalyst demo); Analysing and Interpreting Data (compare foam heights of 0, 0, 0.5 and 9 cm); Constructing Explanations (use collision theory and activation energy); Developing and Using Models (add the catalyst to the particle model). Also observing, measuring (foam height in cm), communicating and collaborating.
slo.attitudes: Values (KICD): Responsibility and Respect: carefully uses materials and respects others' opinions during group discussion of factors affecting the rate of reactions. Appreciates the importance of manipulating factors affecting the rate of chemical and biological processes in day-to-day life. Core competencies: Communication and collaboration; Digital literacy (research on optimum conditions in biological, chemical and physical processes). PCI: Safety and security: observes safety measures when carrying out activities to investigate rates of reactions.
slo.keyInquiry: How do various factors affect the rate of reactions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 3 to 5 the only factors were temperature, concentration and surface area, each changing the frequency or energy of collisions. Here learners meet a rate change with no change in temperature, concentration or size, which challenges the model and pushes it forward: a catalyst lowers the activation energy so a larger fraction of collisions are effective. This prepares Lesson 7 (optimum conditions for enzymes) and Lesson 8 (final model).
slo.safetyNotes: Wear goggles. 3% hydrogen peroxide can irritate eyes and skin; rinse any splash with plenty of water. Teacher handles the peroxide and the liver. Wash hands after touching raw liver and keep it away from the mouth. Use a tray under the measuring cylinders for foam overflow. Boil the liver cube in advance with teacher supervision only. Dispose of the liver and solutions as the teacher directs. No tasting of any material. For the discussion, note that SO2 from the anchor reaction is an irritant, so that reaction is not repeated here.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng returns to the Disappearing Cross: warm Beaker B (50 C) was 7.7 times faster than cold Beaker A (10 C), 35 s versus 270 s, with identical chemicals. Lessons 3 to 5 gave temperature, concentration and surface area, all of which change how often or how energetically particles collide. Today Wanjiru, Otieno, Amina and Kiprono's groups meet a puzzle: 10 cm3 of 3% hydrogen peroxide with a few drops of detergent shows no foam on its own, yet a 1 cm3 cube of fresh liver makes a column of foam 9 cm high within 30 s at the same temperature, concentration and amount. Learners predict, observe the four set-ups (no additive, sand, boiled liver, fresh liver), find that the liver is not used up, and explain using catalyst, enzyme (catalase) and lower activation energy via an alternative pathway. They then discuss the Haber process (iron catalyst for ammonia, used worldwide; Kenya imports and blends fertiliser, for example at Athi River) and light as an energy source in photosynthesis, distinguishing light from a catalyst. The class adds new questions to the DQB and revises the cumulative particle model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the anchor: both beakers had the same chemicals, and the cross vanished at 35 s (Beaker B, 50 C) and 270 s (Beaker A, 10 C). They list the factors found so far (temperature, concentration, surface area) and what each changes about collisions. Then Mwalimu Achieng shows four measuring cylinders, each with 10 cm3 of 3% hydrogen peroxide and a few drops of detergent, at the same room temperature, labelled: no additive, sand, boiled liver cube, fresh liver cube (each cube 1 cm3). Individually in their science notebooks, learners predict the foam height after 30 s for each cylinder and write a reason, then compare with a partner. They also write: Can a reaction speed up if temperature, concentration and piece size do not change?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last week we found three ways to change how many collisions are effective each second. Turn to your notebook: which factors have we found, and what does each do to the particles?' Take answers from 3 learners by cold-call (include Wanjiru and Kiprono). Hold up the four cylinders: 'The same peroxide, the same temperature, the same amount. Only the thing I drop in is different. Predict the foam height after 30 seconds for each, and give a reason.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds in silence while they write. Then say: 'Turn to your partner for 1 minute and compare.' Cold-call 4 pairs for different predictions and write them on the board without judging. Ask: 'Which of the three factors could explain a difference here? If none can, what does that tell us?' Wait 10 seconds. Link to the phenomenon: 'If a fourth factor exists, it should help explain the Disappearing Cross too.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction before evidence) combined with eliciting prior knowledge. Writing a prediction with a reason commits learners to a model, so that surprise at the fresh liver result creates cognitive conflict and motivates revising collision theory. Asking whether any known factor explains the difference makes learners test the existing model against a new case.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for: (1) a prediction for each of the four cylinders with a reason; (2) correct recall of temperature, concentration and surface area with their effect on collisions; (3) whether learners attribute differences to a known factor (misconception: the liver is hotter or 'adds more peroxide'). Tally on the board how many predict that fresh liver differs from boiled liver. Note learners who say sand will act like liver, and revisit them in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 observe the demonstration, each member with an assigned role (reader, timer, foam measurer, recorder). Mwalimu Achieng adds each additive to its cylinder at the same moment and starts the clock. At 30 s groups measure foam height with a ruler and record: no additive = 0 cm; sand = 0 cm; boiled liver cube = 0.5 cm; fresh liver cube = 9 cm. They identify the independent variable (additive), dependent variable (foam height after 30 s) and control variables (10 cm3 of 3% hydrogen peroxide, detergent, temperature, 1 cm3 cube size, time). They test with a glowing splint held by the teacher that gas given off is oxygen: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2. Groups then lift out the fresh liver cube with forceps, rinse and weigh or look at it, and see it is still there and unchanged in size, then add it to fresh peroxide where it again produces foam. They record these observations in a table and in a sketch with labels.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting say: 'Goggles on. Hydrogen peroxide can irritate your eyes, so only I pour it.' Assign roles: 'Reader, timer, measurer, recorder. Hands up when you know your role.' Say: 'Watch all four cylinders at once. Measure the foam height at exactly 30 seconds and record in centimetres.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which variable did we change? Which did we keep the same? Why is sand in the set-up?' (to show that any solid does not work, so it is not just the solid). Ask: 'Why do we have a boiled liver cube?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Then lift out the fresh liver cube: 'Is the liver still here? Is it smaller? What does that tell us about whether it was used up?' Cold-call 3 learners (include Amina and Otieno). Add the used cube to fresh peroxide: 'Predict, then watch.' Link to the phenomenon: 'Nothing about the temperature, concentration or size of the peroxide changed. Yet the rate changed enormously.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with variable identification (fair-test design from Lesson 2). Contrasting cases (sand, boiled liver, fresh liver) isolate the cause: not just any solid, and not liver whose enzyme has been destroyed by boiling. Reusing the liver gives direct evidence that it is not used up, building the defining feature of a catalyst from observation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (1) record 0, 0, 0.5 and 9 cm correctly with units; (2) correctly name independent, dependent and at least four control variables; (3) use the same time for every cylinder; (4) wear goggles and keep the tray under the cylinders. Ask a group member to explain why the boiled liver result differs from fresh liver (look for: boiling damages the enzyme). Learners who say liver 'reacted and disappeared' need to be redirected to the evidence from the retrieved cube.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners construct a written explanation answering: Why did the fresh liver cube make 9 cm of foam while sand made 0 cm and boiled liver made 0.5 cm, with the same temperature, concentration and amount of peroxide? Mwalimu Achieng introduces the terms catalyst, enzyme, catalase and activation energy. Learners use a simple energy diagram to show the reaction pathway without a catalyst (high energy hill) and with a catalyst (alternative pathway, lower hill), and link to collision theory: more collisions have enough energy to be effective, so the rate rises, though the particles' speed has not changed. Next, they discuss in groups: (a) the Haber process, where an iron catalyst helps make ammonia, used worldwide for fertiliser (Kenya imports and blends fertiliser, for example blending at Athi River; no Haber plant is claimed there); (b) photosynthesis, where light supplies energy and is not a catalyst; silver bromide in photographic film changes in light. They return to the Disappearing Cross and decide what a catalyst would change in Beaker A. They also connect to digestion: the gut uses enzymes so that food breaks down quickly at body temperature.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use the words particles, collisions and activation energy. In two minutes write why fresh liver made 9 cm of foam and sand made none.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before anyone speaks, then a pair share. Cold-call 3 learners to read explanations; ask others: 'Do you agree? What would you add?' Introduce terms: 'Activation energy is the minimum energy a collision needs to react. A catalyst gives the reaction an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions are effective, and the catalyst is not used up. An enzyme is a biological catalyst; the enzyme in liver is catalase.' Draw both pathways and ask: 'Did the catalyst make the particles hotter? Did it add more particles?' (No.) Correct misconceptions: 'A catalyst does not make more product; both cylinders would end with the same amount of oxygen, only the time differs.' For light: 'Light supplies energy; it is not a catalyst. Leaves in Kericho tea fields use light for photosynthesis.' Discuss Haber: 'Why would industry want an iron catalyst?' Cold-call 3 groups. Return to the anchor: 'Explain to a partner in one sentence how temperature and a catalyst each speed up a reaction but in different ways.' (Temperature gives particles more energy; a catalyst lowers the energy needed.) Add: 'In the gut, catalase-like enzymes work at body temperature, so a lower activation energy matters.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a visual model (energy pathway diagram). Learners must cite the 0, 0, 0.5 and 9 cm data as evidence and use activation energy as reasoning. Compare-and-contrast of two ways to increase effective collisions (more energy by heating versus a lower energy requirement by a catalyst) strengthens the unified collision-theory idea. Applying the idea to the Haber process and photosynthesis transfers it to new contexts and separates catalysts from light.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for written explanations that: (1) cite the data (9 cm versus 0 cm and 0.5 cm); (2) state that the catalyst gives an alternative pathway with lower activation energy; (3) say more collisions are effective; (4) say the catalyst is not used up and does not change the final amount of product; (5) state that light is an energy source, not a catalyst. Misconceptions to track: 'catalyst adds energy', 'catalyst is a reactant', 'boiled liver still works a little because it is a catalyst' (it is a damaged enzyme). Use a quick thumbs-up/down check: 'A catalyst is used up in the reaction.' Ask 4 learners to justify their response.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups return to the DQB on the back wall. They (1) place an answer card on questions from Lesson 1 that can now be partly answered (for example, whether something other than temperature can change the speed); (2) write new questions on sticky notes arising from today, such as: Can a catalyst help Beaker A? Why does boiling stop the liver working? Do catalysts work in cars? How do enzymes in the stomach work at body temperature? Does the Haber process need heat as well? Is light needed for all reactions? Learners place notes under headings: Temperature, Concentration, Surface area, Catalysts, Light, and Other. Kiprono adds a question about whether the enzymes in fermenting uji behave like catalase; Amina adds one about whether anything slows rusting of roofing sheets in Mombasa. These are flagged for Lesson 7.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go to the DQB. Find one question we can now answer with evidence and one new question that today raised.' Allow 3 minutes. Cold-call 4 groups to read one card and one new question aloud. Ask: 'What evidence do we have for that answer? Is it complete?' Wait 10 seconds. Sort questions with the class: 'Which can we answer from today's data? Which need Lesson 7 or 8?' Praise specificity. Challenge vague questions: 'Can you make it testable? What would you change and what would you measure?' Link to the driving question: 'How does what we learned today help make life in Kenya safer, healthier and more productive?' Mention enzyme action in digestion, fertiliser supply and photosynthesis in crops.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding. Linking new questions to evidence shows how investigation produces further questions, and sorting them into factors keeps the focus on the central question, which keeps learners accountable for tracing each answer back to data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that: (1) answer cards cite evidence from today (such as 9 cm versus 0 cm) and not opinion; (2) new questions are about catalysts, light or energy in reactions; (3) at least one question from each group is testable; (4) learners can say which questions are not yet answerable. Record names of learners whose questions show deeper reasoning (for example asking about enzymes and temperature) for extension in Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners revise their cumulative particle model for the Disappearing Cross. Their model page from earlier lessons shows particles of thiosulfate and HCl, with changes for temperature, concentration and surface area. Today they add a fourth component: a catalyst, drawn as an alternative energy pathway with lower activation energy, and a note that light can supply energy in some reactions. They draw a labelled sketch of an energy diagram for the hydrogen peroxide reaction with and without catalase, and a particle sketch showing more effective collisions with the catalyst. Then they complete a statement: 'In the Disappearing Cross, the 50 C beaker was faster than the 10 C beaker (35 s versus 270 s) because ... A catalyst would speed a reaction in a different way by ...'. They finish with a short written exit ticket.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open to your model page. Add one new idea today: what does a catalyst do to the energy needed for effective collisions? Include a labelled diagram.' Circulate for 5 minutes and ask: 'Where did you show the lower activation energy? Is the catalyst in the products?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Choose 2 models to show (with permission), one with a clear energy diagram, and ask the class to give a glow (what is strong) and a grow (what to add). Cold-call 3 learners: 'Finish this: the warm beaker was 7.7 times faster than the cold beaker because ...' and then 'A catalyst works differently because ...'. Hand out the exit ticket: 'In two sentences, explain why fresh liver made 9 cm of foam and boiled liver made 0.5 cm. Name the type of molecule in liver.' Close: 'Next lesson we apply all four factors to Kenyan life: enzymes in the gut, fermenting uji, rusting and preserving fish.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with peer critique (glow and grow). Adding a new element to a persisting model shows how new evidence refines an explanation, and drawing both the energy diagram and particle picture links the symbolic level to the particle level. Contrasting temperature with catalyst in the same sentence consolidates that there are two different routes to more effective collisions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model rubric: (a) energy diagram has two labelled pathways with a lower activation energy for the catalyst; (b) states that the catalyst is not used up; (c) explains that more collisions are effective; (d) light shown as an energy source; (e) correct link back to the Disappearing Cross with 35 s and 270 s. Exit ticket: success means naming the enzyme (catalase/protein) and explaining that boiling damaged it. Learners who write that the catalyst 'gives energy' or 'changes the products' need a quick conference at the start of Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Did learners notice that the rate rose without any change in temperature, concentration or particle size, and did the surprise lead them to revise the model rather than dismiss the result? Which learners said the liver was 'used up', and did retrieving the cube change their thinking? Were learners able to separate how a catalyst works (lower activation energy) from how heating works (more energy), and did anyone confuse light with a catalyst? Which DQB questions need Lesson 7 (optimum temperature and pH for enzymes, boiling denatures catalase) and Lesson 8? Check the safety routine: goggles worn, peroxide handled only by the teacher, hands washed after liver.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In 30 s, 10 cm3 of 3% hydrogen peroxide with a few drops of detergent produced foam of 0 cm with no additive, 0 cm with sand, 0.5 cm with a boiled liver cube and 9 cm with a fresh liver cube (1 cm3 each). The fresh liver cube was still there afterwards and worked again in new peroxide. Temperature, concentration and amount were the same in every cylinder.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up and does not change the final amount of product. The enzyme catalase in fresh liver is a biological catalyst; boiling damages it. Light is an energy source for some reactions (photosynthesis) and is not a catalyst. Catalysts are used in industry, such as the iron catalyst in the Haber process for ammonia.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: A catalyst gives the reaction an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy to be effective collisions, and the rate rises without changing temperature, concentration or size. This adds to the Disappearing Cross story: warm Beaker B (35 s) beat cold Beaker A (270 s) because heating gives particles more energy, while a catalyst lowers the energy needed.

LESSONS.title: Applying the Model to Biological, Chemical and Physical Processes in Kenya
LESSONS.aresKeywords: optimum conditions, enzyme, amylase, pepsin, pH, fermentation, preservation, refrigeration, drying, salting, rusting, collision theory, effective collisions, activation energy, rate

slo.purpose: Learners apply the collision-theory model built in Lessons 3 to 6 to real Kenyan systems. They see that several factors act together, that enzymes have optimum conditions, and that preservation works by slowing reactions.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) explain factors that influence the rate of reactions in biological, chemical and physical processes; (b) describe why enzymes such as amylase (near 37 C, pH 7) and pepsin (near pH 2) work best at optimum conditions; (c) explain how cooling, drying and salting slow reactions that spoil food; (d) appreciate the importance of manipulating factors affecting the rate of chemical and biological processes in day-to-day life.
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP 4); Constructing explanations (SEP 6); Developing and using models (SEP 2); Engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7); Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (SEP 8).
slo.attitudes: Respect for others' opinions during group discussion; responsibility when using food and materials; appreciation of how science improves food safety and livelihoods in Kenya. Core competencies: Communication and collaboration; Critical thinking and problem solving. PCIs: Safety and security; Socio-economic issues (food preservation).
slo.keyInquiry: How do various factors affect the rate of reactions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3 to 6 gave the model that rate depends on how many effective collisions happen per second: temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts and light. Lesson 7 moves the model out of the beaker into Kenyan life, such as the gut, uji, roofing sheets and fish at Lake Victoria. It also revisits the Lesson 1 DQB questions, including why Beaker B (35 s) was faster than Beaker A (270 s), and prepares for the Lesson 8 final model.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only food-grade materials, and do not taste anything made in the laboratory. Wash hands before and after handling uji, salt and fish pieces. Wear goggles if any iron nails and salt solution are used. Keep the tutorial paper-based or use samples prepared in advance. Wipe up spills at once. No thiosulfate-HCl reaction is repeated, so SO2 is not a risk in this lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng reopens the Disappearing Cross. Beaker B, at 50 C, lost its cross at 35 s, and Beaker A, at 10 C, lost it at 270 s, so B was 7.7 times faster with identical chemicals. Learners predict what happens to reactions in real Kenyan systems when conditions change: uji left in a warm kitchen at 30 C versus a cool place at 15 C, enzymes in the gut, iron roofing sheets in Mombasa, and fish at Lake Victoria. They analyse reference values (amylase near 37 C and pH 7, pepsin near pH 2, uji 24 h at 30 C versus 48 h at 15 C, fridge 4 C) and revisit the Lesson 3 temperature table as evidence for cooling food. They explain why enzymes have an optimum, how cooling, drying and salting slow spoilage, and that several factors act together. They then review the Lesson 1 DQB questions and revise the class model. The factors change the speed of a reaction, not the final amount made.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the Beaker A / Beaker B record in their science notebooks (10 C, 270 s; 50 C, 35 s). Mwalimu Achieng shows the scenario cards: (1) uji in a warm kitchen at 30 C versus 15 C, (2) a fridge at 4 C holding milk and meat, (3) fresh fish drying in the sun at Lake Victoria. In pairs, learners predict in their notebooks: 'Which will spoil or react faster, and why?' They draw one particle sketch showing what changes in the warm and cool cases. Wanjiru's earlier 'why' question is read aloud to link back to the beaker.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last time we saw the cross vanish at 35 seconds in warm Beaker B and at 270 seconds in cold Beaker A. Today we ask whether the same idea explains uji, a fridge and fish.' Show the three cards and give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before any talk. Then say: 'Write your prediction and one particle sketch first.' Cold-call 4 learners (Wanjiru, Otieno, Amina, Kiprono, or other learners using the same role names) to share predictions without correcting them. Say: 'Do not tell me if it is right yet. Tell me what you think the particles are doing.' Record every prediction on chart paper for revisiting at the end.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a particle sketch: committing to a prediction and a mechanism before seeing evidence exposes learners' current model of collisions and creates a clear reason to test it against the data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) predictions that name a direction (warmer spoils faster) and not just 'it changes'; (2) sketches showing particles moving faster or colliding more in the warm case; (3) learners who use the words 'particles' or 'collisions'. Tally how many of the 4 cold-called learners link their reasoning to temperature. Note learners who say a fridge 'stops' reactions, as a misconception to address in Explain.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive a data pack with the Lesson 7 reference values. Part A (temperature and food): uji ferments in about 24 h at 30 C but about 48 h at 15 C; a fridge is at 4 C. Learners reopen the Lesson 3 temperature table (10 C = 270 s, rate 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1; 25 C = 110 s, rate 9.1; 40 C = 52 s, rate 19.2; 55 C = 26 s, rate 38.5) and compare how rate changes with temperature. Part B (enzymes): they read a simple set of approximate classroom values: amylase works best near 37 C and pH 7, and pepsin in the stomach works best near pH 2. They draw a sketch graph of rate (y-axis) against temperature or pH (x-axis) for amylase, showing rate rising to a peak near 37 C and then falling. Part C (preservation): they examine sample cards or pictures of dried and salted fish from Lake Victoria, of sun-drying, and of rusting iron roofing sheets in Mombasa (Amina's example), and list what condition is being changed in each case.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate and ask: 'Which row of the Lesson 3 table is closest to your kitchen? What happens to the time when temperature drops?' Ask groups: 'The uji takes 24 hours at 30 C and 48 hours at 15 C. How many times longer is that, and what does that tell you about the rate?' (Expect: 2 times longer, so the rate is about half.) Say: 'Use evidence from the table, not just opinion.' Prompt: 'Amylase is a biological catalyst, and a catalyst speeds up a reaction. So why does its rate fall if we keep heating above 37 C?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups. Say: 'Do not give me the answer yet. Point to the part of your graph where the rate changes direction.' Remind groups that the final amount of product is not the focus; the speed is.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data analysis with a sketch graph and gallery comparison: converting reference values into rates and plotting a peak shape lets learners notice patterns (steady rise for ordinary reactions, a peak for enzymes) and stops them from assuming 'hotter is always faster'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners (1) calculate the 24 h versus 48 h comparison correctly (2 times, rate about half); (2) quote the 10 C and 25 C rows of the Lesson 3 table to support 'cooler means slower'; (3) draw the enzyme graph with a peak and not a straight line; (4) list the condition changed for each preservation case (cooling, drying, salting). Use a checklist for each group. Ask learners who draw a straight line to point to the 37 C value on the graph.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group builds a written explanation for one case using the collision-theory model: (a) uji at 30 C versus 15 C; (b) why a fridge at 4 C slows spoilage; (c) why amylase and pepsin have different optimum conditions; (d) why drying and salting fish stop spoilage; (e) why iron roofing sheets rust faster in Mombasa than in a dry area (more moisture and salt, and a warm climate). Learners use a claim-evidence-reasoning frame: Claim, Evidence (a number or table row), Reasoning (particles, effective collisions, activation energy, kinetic energy). They also decide which of the four factors (temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst) is acting in each case and note when several act together, for example in the gut: body temperature of 37 C, chewed food (larger surface area), enzymes (catalysts) and a suitable pH. Kiprono links this to uji and tea from Kericho. Groups present in 90 seconds each.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Every explanation must include one number and the word particles.' Model once: 'At 15 C the uji particles have less kinetic energy, so fewer collisions have enough energy to react. This is fewer effective collisions per second, so 48 hours.' Then ask: 'Which factors are acting together in your case?' Introduce the idea that an enzyme has a shape that works best at its optimum pH and temperature; outside it, the enzyme works poorly or stops (too hot changes its shape, so it no longer catalyses). Clarify the misconception: 'A fridge slows the reaction; it does not stop it, and drying and salting remove water that microorganisms and reactions need.' Cold-call 5 learners to restate another group's reasoning in their own words. Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Do not re-teach the individual factors, only link them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with group presentations and peer restatement: tying every claim to a data point and a particle-level mechanism builds the habit of argument from evidence and shows that one model explains many contexts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) the claim states a direction and a comparison; (2) evidence quotes a value exactly (24 h / 48 h, 37 C, pH 2, or a row of the temperature table); (3) reasoning uses 'effective collisions', 'kinetic energy' or 'activation energy' correctly; (4) learners identify at least two factors acting together in the gut. Score each group 0-3 on claim, evidence, reasoning. Listen for the misconception 'the fridge stops the reaction' and for 'more heat always speeds up an enzyme'.

framework.learnerExperience: At the back wall, learners and Mwalimu Achieng review the Lesson 1 DQB questions, including Wanjiru's 'why did Beaker B finish so much faster?' and the questions about mango rotting, ugali cooking, uji and rusting. In groups, learners decide which questions can now be answered, write the answer on a sticky note with the evidence, and move the note beside the question. They add new questions, for example 'Why do some foods keep longer when salted?' and 'Why does a fever change how body reactions work?' Unanswered questions are marked for Lesson 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let us go back to the first questions we put up. Which of them can we answer with evidence today?' Hand out sticky notes and ask each group to move at least one answer to the board. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners to read a question and its answer aloud. Ask: 'What evidence supports that answer? Which lesson gave it to us?' Ask Amina and Kiprono to link the rusting and uji questions to their examples. Circle any question that still has no evidence and say: 'We will use these in Lesson 8.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board revisit: matching earlier questions to the evidence gathered makes learning progress visible and shows learners that the whole sequence is moving toward answering the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group has moved at least one note and attached evidence, not just a statement. Look for answers that cite a lesson (for example 'Lesson 3 table: 10 C = 270 s') and for new questions that show deeper thinking about optimum conditions or preservation. Count the questions answered and the questions left open.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their individual particle model of the Disappearing Cross and revise it. They add a section titled 'Real systems in Kenya' with at least three annotated examples (uji, enzymes in the gut, preserved fish or a fridge) showing which factor changes effective collisions per second. They add a note on optimum conditions: an enzyme has a best temperature and pH (amylase near 37 C and pH 7; pepsin near pH 2). They add a note that cooling, drying and salting slow reactions, and that the factors change the speed, not the final amount of product made. They then compare their first prediction with their revised model and write one sentence: 'I used to think ..., now I think ... because ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open the model you started in Lesson 1. Add what you can now explain, and cross out any idea the evidence does not support.' Display the sentence frame: 'Because ___ (factor), particles ___, so ___ effective collisions per second, so the rate is ___.' Walk around and prompt: 'Which factor is acting here? Where is the evidence?' Pair learners for a 2-minute peer review and give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before they respond. Cold-call 3 learners to read their revision sentence. Return to the beaker and ask: 'If the final model must explain both Beaker B (35 s) and the fridge, what idea do they share?' Expect: more or fewer effective collisions per second because particles have more or less kinetic energy.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with before-and-after comparison: updating the same model each lesson and stating what changed makes learners' reasoning visible and helps them see one mechanism explaining the beaker, the gut and the kitchen.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that (1) include at least three Kenyan examples linked to a named factor; (2) use 'effective collisions' and 'activation energy' correctly; (3) show an optimum for enzymes and not a simple rise; (4) state that final amount is unchanged. Collect the 'I used to think ... now I think ...' sentences as an exit ticket and sort them into secure, developing and misconception piles to plan Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners explain the enzyme peak with particles and shape, or did they just say 'too hot kills it'? Which learners still think a fridge stops reactions completely? Did groups quote a number from the Lesson 3 table and the 24 h / 48 h values? Were at least two factors linked together in the gut example? Which DQB questions remain unanswered, and which will be used in the Lesson 8 assessment? Note any learners who need support with sketching graphs or with using 'effective collisions' accurately.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We looked at the Beaker A / Beaker B result (10 C = 270 s; 50 C = 35 s) and compared it with Kenyan examples: uji fermenting in about 24 h at 30 C but about 48 h at 15 C, a fridge at 4 C, amylase working best near 37 C and pH 7, pepsin near pH 2, dried and salted fish, and rusting roofing sheets in Mombasa.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Several factors act together in real systems. Enzymes (biological catalysts) have optimum temperature and pH. Cooling, drying and salting slow the reactions that spoil food. The factors change the speed of a reaction, not the final amount made.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Because cooler conditions give particles less kinetic energy, fewer collisions have enough energy (activation energy) to react, so there are fewer effective collisions per second and the rate is lower. Enzymes work best when their shape suits the temperature and pH. Drying and salting remove the water needed for spoilage reactions, so food keeps longer.

LESSONS.title: Model Building, Assessment and Community Connection: The Final Explanation
LESSONS.aresKeywords: rate of reaction, collision theory, effective collisions, activation energy, temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst, enzyme, final explanation, model revision

slo.purpose: To let learners put the cumulative collision-theory model to use: to explain the anchor demonstration in full, predict and explain an unfamiliar Kenyan scenario, and choose which factor to change to solve a real problem.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: a) describe rate of chemical reactions (rate = 1/t for the cross method; cm3/s for the gas method); c) explain factors that influence the rate of reactions in biological, chemical and physical processes (temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst, light) using effective collisions and activation energy; d) appreciate the importance of manipulating factors affecting the rate of chemical and biological processes in day-to-day life. Final explanation of the anchor: Beaker B (50 C) cross vanished at 35 s and Beaker A (10 C) at 270 s, so B was 7.7 times faster (rates 28.6 and 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1). Same chemicals, same amounts, only temperature differed. Both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur; factors change the speed, not the final amount made.
slo.skills: Constructing a scientific explanation (claim, evidence, reasoning); using data from earlier tables as evidence (temperature table 25 C = 110 s, 40 C = 52 s; concentration table 0.15 mol/dm3 = 110 s and 0.06 mol/dm3 = 275 s; surface area table initial rates 0.40, 0.93 and 2.07 cm3/s); comparing the Lesson 1 model with the final model; predicting from a model; choosing and justifying a factor to change in a real problem; communicating a message to the community.
slo.attitudes: Responsibility and respect (KICD values): listening to and building on classmates' reasoning during the gallery walk and critique. Appreciation of how controlling reaction rate makes life in Kenya safer, healthier and more productive (food preservation, digestion, cooking, protecting roofing). Curiosity: valuing the questions that remain open on the DQB. Safety and security (PCI): safe handling of any materials and ventilation.
slo.keyInquiry: How do various factors affect the rate of reactions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson. In Lesson 1 learners saw the cross vanish at 35 s in warm Beaker B and 270 s in cold Beaker A and could only say 'heat makes it faster'. Lessons 2 to 7 gave them rate = 1/t and fair tests (L2), temperature and first collision theory (L3), concentration (L4), surface area (L5), catalysts and light (L6) and optimum conditions in Kenyan systems (L7). Now they bring everything together in a Final Explanation of the anchor, close out the DQB, compare their first and final models, and show they can use the model on a new problem.
slo.safetyNotes: No new chemical work is required. If Beakers A and B are re-shown, use the same small quantities (10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate), a ventilated room, goggles, and rinse beakers straight after the cross vanishes because SO2 is an irritant. Prefer showing the L1 notebook records or a replay instead of repeating the demo. For the transfer task use only paper-based or safe household examples (no heating of oil, no open flames beyond what is normal in a school kitchen). Keep walkways clear for the gallery walk.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Achieng opens by asking the class to predict, in their science notebooks, what they now think a particle-level picture of Beakers A and B looks like and how they would solve an unfamiliar Kenyan problem: a trader in Kisumu whose fresh fish spoils in hours, and a farmer in Kericho choosing how to speed up composting of tea waste. Learners revisit the anchor evidence (35 s vs 270 s, 7.7 times faster, rates 28.6 and 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1) and write a full Final Explanation using claim, evidence and reasoning, citing one row from the temperature, concentration or surface area tables. They apply the same model to the new scenario, with no new numbers, deciding which factor to change and why. Wanjiru, Otieno, Amina and Kiprono's DQB questions are sorted into answered, partly answered and still open. Learners then compare their Lesson 1 model with a final class model, noting what changed, and finish with a short community message about controlling reaction rates and a link to careers such as KEMRI biochemists.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their notebooks to the Lesson 1 page on which they recorded the anchor observation (Beaker B cross gone at 35 s, Beaker A at 270 s). Individually (3 minutes) they sketch a particle-level picture of each beaker and write a prediction for a NEW problem with no numbers: 'A fish trader in Kisumu wants her tilapia to stay fresh for a whole day without a fridge. Which factor would you change, in which direction, and what will happen to the rate of the spoiling reactions?' They then pair up with a partner and compare predictions, noting where they used words like particles, collisions and energy.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng says: 'Open to your Lesson 1 page. Two beakers, same chemicals, same amounts. Draw what you now think the particles are doing in A and in B. Then tell me how you would slow spoilage of fish at Lake Victoria.' She gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silence before pairs talk. She circulates and cold-calls 4 learners (including Wanjiru and Kiprono) to read one prediction aloud without correction, saying: 'Thank you. I am not telling you if it is right yet. We will test it with evidence.' She records 3 predictions on the board under 'Our predictions before the final explanation'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-before-instruction with an individual-then-pair 'Think-Pair-Share': learners commit to a prediction first, so they can later see for themselves how their thinking has changed. It also activates their prior model from Lessons 1 to 7 so the Explain phase builds on their own ideas rather than the teacher's.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) sketches with particles drawn moving faster or more crowded in B, not just a label 'hot'; (2) use of the words 'particles' and 'collide' in at least half of the predictions; (3) any prediction that names a factor (temperature, drying, salting, surface area) for the fish. Tally on a class list how many learners link their fish prediction to collisions. Learners who give only 'because it is cold' receive a prompt in the Explain phase: 'What are the particles doing?'

framework.learnerExperience: Evidence review in groups of four. Each group receives a printed 'Evidence Pack' with only data already collected: the anchor result (A: 270 s, rate 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1; B: 35 s, rate 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1; 7.7 times faster; 235 s difference), the temperature table (10 C = 270 s, 25 C = 110 s, 40 C = 52 s, 55 C = 26 s), the concentration table (0.15 to 0.06 mol/dm3 giving 110 to 275 s, rate/concentration about 60), the surface area initial rates (0.40, 0.93, 2.07 cm3/s; maximum 120 cm3), the catalyst foam heights (0, 0, 0.5, 9 cm) and the Lesson 7 values (amylase near 37 C and pH 7; pepsin near pH 2; uji 24 h at 30 C vs 48 h at 15 C; fridge 4 C). Groups highlight patterns in two colours: 'what changed' and 'what stayed the same'. Each group notes that both beakers produce the same final amount of sulfur and that the factors changed only how fast. They also look at the new scenario (fish at Lake Victoria dried, salted or kept cold; tea waste composted in Kericho) and list which factors are present in each.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng says: 'You are detectives. Find ONE row of data that best explains why Beaker B was faster, and be ready to defend it.' She hands out packs and sets a 10-minute timer. She asks groups: 'In the anchor, what was kept the same? What was different?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. She cold-calls 3 groups to name their chosen row and says: 'Why did you pick that one over the others?' She reminds them to use only the given numbers and not invent any new ones. She points to the DQB and says: 'Which of these numbers answers one of our questions?' Where groups mix up rate and time she asks: 'Is a bigger rate a longer time or a shorter time?' She also checks that no group claims a factor changes the final amount of product.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence sorting with a 'same / different' highlight: learners identify control and independent variables across all earlier investigations, which shows that the same particle idea runs through every factor. Looking across four datasets lets learners see the pattern (more effective collisions per second means a higher rate) instead of seeing seven separate facts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: groups correctly identify temperature as the only difference between Beakers A and B; at least one row quoted accurately (for example 40 C = 52 s or 0.06 mol/dm3 = 275 s); groups can state that the amount of sulfur at the end is the same. Use a quick checklist per group. If a group misquotes a value, send them back to the pack. Reteach later if two or more groups confuse rate with time.

framework.learnerExperience: Part 1 (individual, 10 minutes): Each learner writes a FINAL EXPLANATION of the anchor in their notebook using the frame: CLAIM (why was Beaker B faster?), EVIDENCE (35 s vs 270 s, 7.7 times faster, rates 28.6 vs 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1, plus one row from the temperature, concentration or surface area table), REASONING (particles, kinetic energy, collisions, effective collisions, activation energy, and that the same amount of sulfur forms in the end). Part 2 (groups, 10 minutes): Learners then use the model on the new scenario: 'In Kisumu, a trader dries and salts fish; in Kericho, Kiprono's family wants tea-leaf waste to compost faster. Which factor would you change and why?' They write a reasoned recommendation, for example: cooling or drying fish lowers the rate of spoilage reactions, as shown by the temperature table (lower temperature gives fewer effective collisions per second); chopping the tea waste increases surface area and warmth increases the rate, like the powder at 2.07 cm3/s versus large chips at 0.40 cm3/s. Part 3: Pairs swap explanations and use a peer checklist to give one 'star' and one 'step'.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng models the frame with a sentence starter on the board: 'Beaker B was faster because ... The evidence is ... This happens because ...'. She says: 'A good explanation uses the words particles, energy, collide and effective. Which of these will you use first?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. She asks Otieno, Amina, Kiprono and Wanjiru (4 cold-calls) to share one sentence from their reasoning, linking to their own earlier contributions: Otieno's particle idea (L1), Amina's rusting roof, Kiprono's uji and tea, Wanjiru's first 'why'. She probes: 'Does higher temperature only mean more collisions, or also something about energy?' and 'Did the factors change how much sulfur was made, or how fast?' She corrects misconceptions: 'frequency of collisions' is not the same as energy of collisions; a catalyst is not used up; light is a source of energy and not a catalyst. She checks that the new scenario uses no new numbers: 'Use only the data in your pack to justify your choice.' She selects 2 strong explanations to read aloud (with permission) and annotates them on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) scientific argumentation, followed by transfer to an unfamiliar scenario. CER forces learners to connect observed data to the particle model, and transfer shows whether they can use the model as a tool rather than recite it. Peer review with 'star and step' builds a shared standard for a good explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 4-point rubric on the notebook explanation: (1) correct claim naming temperature; (2) accurate evidence citing 35 s and 270 s plus one table row; (3) reasoning including kinetic energy, effective collisions and activation energy; (4) recognises that the final amount of sulfur is unchanged. For the new scenario look for a chosen factor, a direction (increase or decrease), and a reason using collisions. A learner at level 2 or below receives a targeted question at the end of the lesson; note names for follow-up. Collect 6 notebooks as exit evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: At the back wall, learners return to the DQB that Mwalimu Achieng has kept since Lesson 1. Working in their groups, each takes 3 to 4 questions (for example Wanjiru's 'Why was B faster if the chemicals are the same?', Amina's question about rusting roofing sheets in Mombasa, Kiprono's question about uji and tea, and the L1 DQB questions revisited in L7). They sort each question with sticky notes into three columns: ANSWERED (with the lesson number and evidence), PARTLY ANSWERED, and STILL OPEN. Each learner then adds one new question they would like to investigate next (for example about pressure, which was named in the KICD list but not investigated here, or about how medicines are stored in hot places). Finally, the class returns to the whole driving question and each group completes the sentence: 'We can control the speed of reactions to make life in Kenya safer, healthier or more productive by ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng says: 'Walk to the board. For each question, point to the data that answers it. If you cannot point to data, it is not yet answered.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before groups move. She cold-calls 3 groups to defend a placement: 'Why do you say this is only partly answered?' She asks Amina to explain her roofing-sheet question in terms of rate and conditions (with L7 content only), and Kiprono to link uji at 30 C vs 15 C (24 h vs 48 h) to the model. She says: 'A question that stays open is not a failure; it is where scientists go next.' She records the new questions in a list headed 'Questions for next time'. She checks that every group has linked at least one answered question to a named lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB sorting and revisiting: classifying questions as answered, partly answered or open makes learning visible and shows learners the growth in their understanding over eight lessons. Writing a new question models the way scientists extend knowledge and gives ownership of what happens next.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: each placement justified with a specific piece of evidence (for example 'answered: L3 temperature table, 40 C = 52 s'); at least one question per group honestly placed as partly answered or open; new questions that are testable and tied to reaction rate. Record the count of questions moved to ANSWERED as a class indicator. If a group places a question as answered without evidence, ask: 'Which row shows that?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out the Lesson 1 model they drew (their first idea of why B was faster) and place it beside a blank page. Working in groups they build the FINAL MODEL on a large sheet: particle diagrams of Beakers A and B showing speed and collisions, with labelled effective collisions, activation energy, and a panel for each factor (temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst, light) showing what changes. They add a note that the amount of sulfur made at the end is the same in both beakers; only the rate differs. They then complete a comparison table: 'Lesson 1 model' vs 'Final model' with rows for What I thought, What I know now, Evidence, and What I still wonder. In the final 8 minutes, each group chooses one real Kenyan problem (fish preservation at Lake Victoria, uji fermentation, rusting roofing sheets in Mombasa, digestion with amylase, fertiliser production with an iron catalyst in the Haber process, which is used worldwide) and prepares a 30-second community message on which factor to change, and why. Groups do a gallery walk, leaving one comment on two other posters. A short closing talk links these ideas to careers, such as biochemists at KEMRI.
framework.teacherMoves: Mwalimu Achieng says: 'Your final model must be able to explain the two beakers AND the fish AND one more case. If it cannot, revise it.' She provides sugar paper, markers and a model checklist (particles, kinetic energy, effective collisions, activation energy, five factors, same final amount). WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before groups begin drawing. She circulates asking: 'Where in your model does the temperature table row show up?' and 'What does your model predict if the fish is dried AND kept cold?' She cold-calls 4 learners during the gallery walk: 'What changed between your first model and this one?' She gives each group 30 seconds for the community message and says: 'Speak to a farmer or trader, not a scientist. Use one factor and one reason.' In the last 3 minutes she invites Wanjiru to read her first 'why' question from L1 and then answer it in her own words. She closes by asking learners to rate their confidence from 1 to 4 in their notebooks and to write one sentence on how reaction rates matter to their own family.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with side-by-side comparison: placing the Lesson 1 model next to the final model makes the change in thinking concrete and builds metacognition. The gallery walk with written comments uses peer feedback, and the community message turns the model into a tool for action, linking science to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators in the final model: (1) both beakers drawn with particle speed and collisions differing; (2) all five factors represented with a correct direction of effect; (3) a correct note that factors change the rate, not the final amount of sulfur; (4) comparison table with at least two substantive changes from Lesson 1; (5) a community message naming one factor, one direction and one collision-based reason. Score each poster with the 4-level rubric (exceeds, meets, approaches, below). Note groups at 'approaches' or below for follow-up in the next lesson. Use the 1 to 4 confidence rating as an exit ticket.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners could explain the anchor using effective collisions and activation energy rather than just 'heat makes it faster'? Did anyone still claim that a factor changes how much sulfur forms, or that a catalyst is used up, or confuse rate with time? Which evidence rows did learners choose most often, and did they quote them accurately without adding new numbers? How did Wanjiru, Otieno, Amina and Kiprono's DQB questions help others to see the link between lessons? Which transfer scenario (fish, tea waste, uji, roofing) produced the strongest reasoning, and which needs more support? What would I change about timing, grouping or the Evidence Pack the next time I teach this sub-strand?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In the anchor demonstration, the cross vanished at 35 s in warm Beaker B (50 C) and at 270 s in cold Beaker A (10 C): 7.7 times faster, with rates 28.6 and 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1. The same chemicals and amounts were used, and both ended with the same amount of sulfur. Add one row of evidence from the temperature, concentration or surface area table.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Reaction rate depends on how many effective collisions happen per second. Higher temperature, higher concentration, larger surface area and a catalyst all increase the rate; light supplies energy for some reactions. Factors change how fast, not how much, product forms. Optimum conditions exist in biological systems, and cooling, drying and salting slow reactions to preserve food.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Write your Final Explanation: Beaker B was faster because at 50 C the particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and with more energy, and a larger fraction of collisions have at least the activation energy, making them effective. Cite your evidence row. Then explain how you would change one factor to solve a real Kenyan problem (for example preserving fish at Lake Victoria) and how your model has changed since Lesson 1.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: General Science Grade 10: 2.5 Rates of Reactions – Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation for the Disappearing Cross. Mwalimu Achieng's class in Nakuru County has been asking: Why do some chemical reactions happen in a flash while others take days, and how can we control the speed of reactions to make life in Kenya safer, healthier and more productive? Use your science notebook, the class data tables and your Driving Question Board (DQB) to help you. Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use full sentences, include numbers with units where you can, and use the words particles, effective collisions and activation energy. Remember the claim, evidence and reasoning structure. In Section 3 you will use a table of results.

sections.title: Section 1: Explain the Disappearing Cross (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning)
sections.prompt:
In the anchor demonstration, 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid was put in each of two beakers and 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate was added. Beaker A was at 10 C and Beaker B was at 50 C. The black cross disappeared at 35 s in one beaker and at 270 s in the other.
(a) Write a CLAIM that answers Wanjiru's question: why did one beaker reach the end point faster than the other?
(b) Give EVIDENCE from the demo: the times, how many times faster, and the rate for each beaker using rate = 1/t.
(c) Write your REASONING using particles, collisions, kinetic energy and activation energy.
(d) State what was the same in both beakers, and what you can say about the amount of sulfur made at the end.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Claim: Warm Beaker B (50 C) reacted faster than cold Beaker A (10 C) because the higher temperature made more of the collisions between particles effective.
(b) Evidence: The cross vanished at 35 s in Beaker B and at 270 s in Beaker A. The difference is 270 - 35 = 235 s, and 270/35 = 7.7, so Beaker B was 7.7 times faster. Rate of B = 1/35 = 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1. Rate of A = 1/270 = 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1.
(c) Reasoning: At 50 C the particles have more kinetic energy. They move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy. A larger fraction of the collisions have at least the activation energy (the minimum energy needed for a collision to react), so there are more effective collisions per second. More effective collisions per second means sulfur forms faster and hides the cross sooner. At 10 C the particles have less energy, so fewer collisions are effective and the cross stays visible longer.
(d) The chemicals, amounts (50 cm3 of thiosulfate, 10 cm3 of HCl), beaker type, cross and observer were the same; only temperature differed. Both beakers end with the same amount of sulfur, because temperature changes the speed of the reaction, not the final amount made.

sections.title: Section 2: Fair Testing and Measuring Rate
sections.prompt:
Amina wants to test whether temperature changes the rate, using the cross method.
(a) Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and at least three control variables for her test.
(b) Amina says: 'I will use a different observer and a bigger beaker for the hot test, because it is faster anyway.' Explain why this plan is not a fair test.
(c) Explain why a shorter time for the cross to disappear gives a bigger rate.
(d) Name two other ways, besides the time for a precipitate to hide a cross, that the rate of a reaction can be measured.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Independent variable: temperature (the factor you change). Dependent variable: the time for the cross to disappear (then the rate, 1/t). Control variables (any three): 50 cm3 of 0.15 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate, 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl, the same type of beaker, the same cross, the same observer, the same lighting.
(b) It is not fair because more than one thing would change: temperature, observer and beaker size. A different observer may judge the cross as gone at a different time, and a different beaker changes the depth of liquid. We could not tell whether temperature or the other changes caused the different time. Only the independent variable should change.
(c) Rate = 1/t. When t is small, 1 divided by t is a bigger number. For example, 1/35 = 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1 is bigger than 1/270 = 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1, so the faster reaction has the bigger rate.
(d) Measure the volume of gas produced over time (rate = volume in cm3 divided by time in s), and measure the loss of mass as a gas escapes.

sections.title: Section 3: Using Evidence from the Tables
sections.prompt:
Here is the class-mean data from Lessons 3 and 4. All used 10 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl and a total thiosulfate volume of 50 cm3.

Temperature test (0.15 mol/dm3 thiosulfate):

| Temperature (C) | Time for cross to disappear (s) | Rate (x10^-3 s^-1) |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 270 | 3.7 |
| 25 | 110 | 9.1 |
| 40 | 52 | 19.2 |
| 55 | 26 | 38.5 |

Concentration test (all at 25 C):

| Sodium thiosulfate (mol/dm3) | Time (s) | Rate (x10^-3 s^-1) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.15 | 110 | 9.1 |
| 0.12 | 138 | 7.2 |
| 0.09 | 183 | 5.5 |
| 0.06 | 275 | 3.6 |

(a) Describe the pattern in rate as temperature rises from 10 C to 55 C.
(b) The anchor demo at 50 C took 35 s. Show whether this fits your pattern in (a).
(c) Describe the pattern between concentration and rate, and use the numbers to say how rate and concentration are related.
(d) Explain the concentration pattern using particles. Why does the energy of the particles not explain it?
sections.exemplar:
(a) The rate increases as temperature rises: 3.7, 9.1, 19.2 and 38.5 x10^-3 s^-1 at 10, 25, 40 and 55 C. From 10 C to 55 C the rate rises from 3.7 to 38.5, about ten times bigger.
(b) The demo time of 35 s at 50 C lies between 52 s at 40 C and 26 s at 55 C, so it fits the pattern: the higher the temperature, the shorter the time.
(c) As concentration falls from 0.15 to 0.06 mol/dm3 the time rises from 110 s to 275 s and the rate falls from 9.1 to 3.6 x10^-3 s^-1. Rate divided by concentration is about 60 in every row (for example 9.1/0.15 is about 61 and 3.6/0.06 = 60), so rate is roughly proportional to concentration.
(d) A higher concentration has more particles in the same volume, so particles collide more often and there are more effective collisions per second. The temperature was 25 C in every test, so the particles had the same kinetic energy and the same activation energy requirement; the energy of the particles did not change.

sections.title: Section 4: Surface Area, Catalysts and Light
sections.prompt:
(a) In Lesson 5, 0.5 g of marble chips (CaCO3) in 25 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 HCl at 25 C gave initial rates over the first 30 s of 0.40 cm3/s for large chips, 0.93 cm3/s for small chips and 2.07 cm3/s for powder. Explain why powder gave the fastest rate, and say what happened to the final volume of CO2 for all three.
(b) In Lesson 6, 10 cm3 of 3% hydrogen peroxide with detergent gave 0 cm of foam with no additive, 0 cm with sand, 0.5 cm with a boiled liver cube and 9 cm with a fresh liver cube after 30 s. Explain why fresh liver made so much foam, using the words catalyst, enzyme and activation energy. Why did the boiled liver not work well?
(c) Kiprono says light is a catalyst. Do you agree? Give a reason and an example.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Powder has a much larger surface area than large chips, so more CaCO3 particles are exposed to HCl particles. There are more effective collisions per second, so CO2 is made faster and the volume-time curve is steeper. The mass of marble, the acid and the temperature were the same, so all three reach the same maximum of about 120 cm3 of CO2; surface area changes the speed, not the final amount.
(b) Fresh liver contains the enzyme catalase, a biological catalyst. It gives the hydrogen peroxide reaction (2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2) an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions are effective and oxygen forms quickly, making 9 cm of foam. The liver is not used up, so it can work again. Boiling damages the enzyme, so the boiled liver gave only 0.5 cm. Sand gave 0 cm, showing that not every solid speeds up the reaction.
(c) I disagree. Light is a source of energy for some reactions, such as photosynthesis in plant leaves; it supplies energy, whereas a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is not used up.

sections.title: Section 5: Solve a Kenyan Problem and Reflect on Your Model
sections.prompt:
A trader in Kisumu finds that her fresh fish from Lake Victoria spoils within hours. A farmer in Kericho wants to speed up composting of tea waste.
(a) For the fish trader, choose one way to slow down spoilage reactions. Explain, using particles and collisions, why it works.
(b) For the Kericho farmer, choose one factor to change to speed up composting. Say how you would change it and explain why it works.
(c) Use the idea of an optimum to explain why the enzyme amylase in your body works best near 37 C and pH 7, and what you would expect if conditions were far from this.
(d) Describe how your particle model has changed since Lesson 1, and state one DQB question that is now answered.
(e) Write one sentence of advice for your community about controlling reaction rates, and name a career that uses this knowledge.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Cool the fish, for example by keeping it in a fridge at 4 C or on ice, or dry and salt it. Cooling gives the particles less kinetic energy, so they collide less often and with less energy. Fewer collisions reach the activation energy, so fewer collisions are effective per second and the spoilage reactions are slower. (Drying and salting remove the water needed for spoilage reactions.) Fish keeps longer.
(b) Increase the surface area by chopping the tea waste into small pieces, or raise the temperature by keeping the compost warm. Smaller pieces expose more particles, so there are more effective collisions per second and the rate rises. Warmth gives particles more kinetic energy, so more collisions are effective.
(c) Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature and pH where their shape suits the reaction. Amylase works best near 37 C and pH 7. Far from these conditions the enzyme's shape is damaged, as with boiled liver, so it works slowly or not at all.
(d) At the start I only had a first sketch of particles and could not say why warm Beaker B was faster. Now my model says rate depends on the number of effective collisions per second, and temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts each change this. Answered DQB question: Why was Beaker B faster than Beaker A? Because at 50 C particles have more kinetic energy, collide more often and with more energy, so more collisions have at least the activation energy.
(e) Advice: keep food cool, dry or salted to make it last longer, because slowing reactions slows spoilage. A career: a KEMRI biochemist.

rubric.criterion: Claim, evidence and reasoning for the anchor phenomenon
rubric.excellent: Gives a clear claim, uses exact data (35 s, 270 s, 7.7 times, rates 28.6 and 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1) and links more kinetic energy, more frequent and energetic collisions, and activation energy to more effective collisions per second.
rubric.proficient: Gives a claim and uses most of the data, with reasoning that mentions collisions and energy but may leave out activation energy or effective collisions.
rubric.developing: Claim is vague or reasoning says only that particles move faster or that the reaction is hotter; little or no data is used.

rubric.criterion: Fair testing and use of rate = 1/t
rubric.excellent: Names independent, dependent and control variables correctly, explains why changing several things is unfair, and correctly explains rate = 1/t.
rubric.proficient: Names most variables and gives a basic reason for fairness; rate = 1/t is used correctly with small gaps in the explanation.
rubric.developing: Confuses variables or does not show why the plan is unfair; rate and time are mixed up.

rubric.excellent: Describes trends accurately with numbers, checks that 35 s fits between 52 s and 26 s, and shows rate roughly proportional to concentration (about 60).
rubric.proficient: Describes trends correctly but with few numbers or without testing proportionality or the 35 s link.
rubric.developing: Misreads the tables or states trends without evidence.

rubric.criterion: Understanding of surface area, catalysts and light
rubric.excellent: Explains surface area, catalysts (lower activation energy, not used up, enzyme) and light correctly, and states that factors change speed, not the final amount.
rubric.proficient: Explains most factors correctly with small gaps, such as missing activation energy or the final amount.
rubric.developing: Mixes up catalysts and light or gives no particle explanation.

rubric.criterion: Applying the model to Kenyan contexts and reflecting
rubric.excellent: Chooses suitable factors for the fish and compost problems, explains them with collision theory, links to optimum conditions for enzymes, and clearly compares the model with Lesson 1.
rubric.proficient: Suggests suitable actions with partial particle explanations and a general reflection.
rubric.developing: Gives actions without reasons, or no reflection on how the model changed.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Why do some chemical reactions happen in a flash while others take days — and how can we control the speed of reactions to make life in Kenya safer, healthier, and more productive?

lessons.title: What Is a Rate of Reaction? Launching the Disappearing Cross
lessons.observed: In the demo, the cross vanished at 35 s in warm Beaker B (50 C) and at 270 s in cold Beaker A (10 C). A yellow precipitate of sulfur formed in both. The chemicals and amounts were the same and only temperature differed, so B was 7.7 times faster.
lessons.learned: Rate of reaction is how fast reactants are used up or products are formed. It can be measured by the time for a change (such as a precipitate hiding a cross), by the volume of gas produced, or by loss of mass.
lessons.explained: So far we can only say that temperature seems linked to speed and that particles may be involved. We have a first particle sketch and DQB questions, but we cannot yet explain why the warm reaction was faster.

lessons.title: Measuring Reaction Rates: Designing a Fair Test
lessons.observed: We calculated the rate for the demo: Beaker B (50 C, 35 s) has rate 1/35 = 28.6 x10^-3 s^-1 and Beaker A (10 C, 270 s) has rate 1/270 = 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1, so B is about 7.7 times faster. Different observers judged the cross gone at slightly different times.
lessons.learned: Rate = 1/t for the cross method, so a shorter time gives a bigger rate. In a fair test we change only the independent variable (temperature), measure the dependent variable (time, then rate) and keep control variables the same (50 cm3 thiosulfate, 10 cm3 HCl, beaker, cross, observer).
lessons.explained: We can compare the two beakers fairly because the chemicals, amounts and way of judging the cross were the same and only temperature differed. We cannot yet explain WHY the warm beaker reacts faster; that question stays on the DQB for Lesson 3.

lessons.title: Factor 1: Temperature
lessons.observed: What did we observe? Record the class-mean times for the cross to disappear at 10 C (270 s), 25 C (110 s), 40 C (52 s) and 55 C (26 s), and the rates 3.7, 9.1, 19.2 and 38.5 x10^-3 s^-1. Note how the demo at 50 C (35 s) fits, and that the amount of sulfur made was the same.
lessons.learned: What did we learn? Write what happens to the rate of the thiosulfate-HCl reaction as temperature rises, and how the rate changes from 10 C to 55 C. State that temperature changes the speed of the reaction and not the final amount of product.
lessons.explained: How can we explain it? Use particles to explain why a higher temperature increases the rate: more kinetic energy, more frequent and more energetic collisions, a larger fraction of effective collisions (activation energy). Use this to explain why warm Beaker B was faster than cold Beaker A.

lessons.title: Factor 2: Concentration
lessons.observed: We observed that at 25 C the cross disappeared in 110 s, 138 s, 183 s and 275 s as the sodium thiosulfate concentration decreased from 0.15 to 0.12, 0.09 and 0.06 mol/dm3. The matching rates (1/t) were 9.1, 7.2, 5.5 and 3.6 x10^-3 s^-1. The weaker the solution, the longer the cross stayed visible.
lessons.learned: We learned that a higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, and that rate is roughly proportional to concentration (rate / concentration is about 60 for every row). Concentration changes how fast the reaction goes, not the type of products, and it is a second factor besides temperature.
lessons.explained: We explained that in a more concentrated solution there are more particles in the same volume, so they collide more often, giving more effective collisions per second and a faster rate. The energy of the particles did not change because the temperature stayed at 25 C. In the anchor demo the concentration was the same in Beakers A and B, so temperature, not concentration, caused the 35 s versus 270 s difference.

lessons.title: Factor 3: Surface Area – Why Does Powder React Faster Than Chunks?
lessons.observed: Powder fizzed fastest and levelled off at 120 cm3 of CO2; small chips were next; large chips were slowest. Initial rates over the first 30 s were 0.40 cm3/s (large), 0.93 cm3/s (small) and 2.07 cm3/s (powder).
lessons.learned: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area, so more particles can collide with acid particles and the rate rises. The gradient of a volume-time curve gives the rate. Surface area changes the speed, not the final amount of gas (maximum about 120 cm3).
lessons.explained: With the same mass, acid and temperature, powder exposes more CaCO3 particles to HCl particles, so there are more effective collisions per second and a steeper curve. This is the same collision idea used for temperature and concentration, and it helps explain why unga cooks faster than whole maize and why a crushed antacid works quickly.

lessons.title: Factor 4: Catalysts and Light
lessons.observed: In 30 s, 10 cm3 of 3% hydrogen peroxide with a few drops of detergent produced foam of 0 cm with no additive, 0 cm with sand, 0.5 cm with a boiled liver cube and 9 cm with a fresh liver cube (1 cm3 each). The fresh liver cube was still there afterwards and worked again in new peroxide. Temperature, concentration and amount were the same in every cylinder.
lessons.learned: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up and does not change the final amount of product. The enzyme catalase in fresh liver is a biological catalyst; boiling damages it. Light is an energy source for some reactions (photosynthesis) and is not a catalyst. Catalysts are used in industry, such as the iron catalyst in the Haber process for ammonia.
lessons.explained: A catalyst gives the reaction an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy to be effective collisions, and the rate rises without changing temperature, concentration or size. This adds to the Disappearing Cross story: warm Beaker B (35 s) beat cold Beaker A (270 s) because heating gives particles more energy, while a catalyst lowers the energy needed.

lessons.title: Applying the Model to Biological, Chemical and Physical Processes in Kenya
lessons.observed: We looked at the Beaker A / Beaker B result (10 C = 270 s; 50 C = 35 s) and compared it with Kenyan examples: uji fermenting in about 24 h at 30 C but about 48 h at 15 C, a fridge at 4 C, amylase working best near 37 C and pH 7, pepsin near pH 2, dried and salted fish, and rusting roofing sheets in Mombasa.
lessons.learned: Several factors act together in real systems. Enzymes (biological catalysts) have optimum temperature and pH. Cooling, drying and salting slow the reactions that spoil food. The factors change the speed of a reaction, not the final amount made.
lessons.explained: Because cooler conditions give particles less kinetic energy, fewer collisions have enough energy (activation energy) to react, so there are fewer effective collisions per second and the rate is lower. Enzymes work best when their shape suits the temperature and pH. Drying and salting remove the water needed for spoilage reactions, so food keeps longer.

lessons.title: Model Building, Assessment and Community Connection: The Final Explanation
lessons.observed: In the anchor demonstration, the cross vanished at 35 s in warm Beaker B (50 C) and at 270 s in cold Beaker A (10 C): 7.7 times faster, with rates 28.6 and 3.7 x10^-3 s^-1. The same chemicals and amounts were used, and both ended with the same amount of sulfur. Add one row of evidence from the temperature, concentration or surface area table.
lessons.learned: Reaction rate depends on how many effective collisions happen per second. Higher temperature, higher concentration, larger surface area and a catalyst all increase the rate; light supplies energy for some reactions. Factors change how fast, not how much, product forms. Optimum conditions exist in biological systems, and cooling, drying and salting slow reactions to preserve food.
lessons.explained: Write your Final Explanation: Beaker B was faster because at 50 C the particles have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and with more energy, and a larger fraction of collisions have at least the activation energy, making them effective. Cite your evidence row. Then explain how you would change one factor to solve a real Kenyan problem (for example preserving fish at Lake Victoria) and how your model has changed since Lesson 1.
